Most of the questions presented for an authoritative opinion, enabling the issues
that had called for a decision to be allayed, were upon matters that had been presented, considered, and decided at former Communications of this Grand Body; and
many were fully covered by the provisions of our Constitution, General Regulations,
etc: A few, however, I deem of sufficient importance to present a compend, as I
could find no precedent in our proceedingil, or in any other Masonic work at my
command,-one at least, having reference to the condition or situation explanatory
of the officers of a Lodge, which was a question of unusual importance to the Lodge,
and required a decision to be promptly given. At the annual election of a Lodge,
the Master elect was re-elected. A Past Master of the Lodge officiating stated that,
as the brother elect was absent from home, he could not be installed, and he would
favor a motion to reconsider the vote, which was done, and another brother elected
as Master. 'l'.hey desired to know if the proceedings were proper. I answered:
"The Master elect, having been duly re-elected, no reconsideration was in order,
tbe first election holding good, without the brother peremptorily declines; if so, a
dispensation will be necessary for another election. It is not essential to install
immediately. See constitutional provision, etc."
I have been asked "If a brother cannot be pot on trial twice for the same
offense?" answering," Our Grand Lodge has decided that a person acquitted on
one trial is no bar to a second trial for the same offense." See Report Committee
on Grievances, our Grand Lodge proceedings, page 317, Vol. III., and pages 311, 363
Vol. IV.
"If a brother under sentence of reprimand by a Lodge in whose jurisdiction he
resides, can be so disciplined when it is ascertained that at the time he is laboring
under the penalty of suspension in his own Lodge?" replied, viz.," Your Lodge has
the right to reprimand the suspended brother; a member of the Fraternity, so careless in his actions whilst under the penalty of suspension in one Lodge, as to incur
reprimand from a Lodge in another jurisdiction, should be expelled from the Order.
Yon will instruct your Secretary to forward a transcript of your trial to the Lodge
suspending the brother, with the statement made herein, that, in my opinion, the
brotherhood will be benefitted by the expulsion of the offender."
I have been requested by one of the Inspectors to give him my views as to the
proper use of the gavel, and informed him "that it is proper and requisite that a
Worshipful Master carry his gavel at funerals and general public occasions, as his
Lodge is under his foll executive control. Being at refreshment, the Marshal is acting subordinate to the direction of the Master, and the brethren must implicitly obey
the gavel on such occasions, thereby enabling the decorum and propriety of their
actions to be fraternally preserved. The brethren are always expected to comply
with and obey the sound of the gavel until they return to the Lodge, and the same
is regularly closed. The gavel, in the Master's hand, should always be obeyed in
the Lodge, whether in the East, before the altar, or any other station." Also, if
"a member of another Lodge, in good standing, can assure the Master that the person elected to receive the degrees in his Lodge is unworthy or in any way disqualified, it i9 his (the Master's) imperative duty to refrain from initiating the person
until" satisfied, by proper investigation, of his status."

when the full value of such established precedents can be rightly estimated, such as
".Annual etections of subordinate Lodge held on the anniversary of St. John the Baptist are not constitutional," etc., etc. "That an initiate, being found unable to read
and write, most learn to do so before advancing." "No person can be invited by
the Masters or Wardens to confer degrees who does not conform to our uniform
work," etc., etc.
The Grand Lodge will have the consideration of the customary amount of amendments to the by-laws of the subordinates for their approval, my action thereon being
but a temporary authorization. Most of those submitted propose a reduction of their
dues; a number desire to change their time of meeting ; a few reduce their fees;
and one increases its fees for the degrees. Two have dropped the obsolete clause of
11 separate ballot for each degree, and conform to the uniform code of by-laws, which
good example, we hope, will be follow,ed by those Lodges still retaining it in their
by-laws. A number were returned, for different reasons, disapproved.
My intercourse with the Lodges during the past year has impressed me with the
view that our country Lodges, in many instances, demand too high a standard for
fees, when the minimum constitutional amount would redound to their interest in
111any particulars. Over half of the Lodges in the State exact the fee of fifty dollars
for the degrees, the balance ranging from sixty to one hundred dollars. I am fully
aware that the subject is a delicate one to broach, considering the financial ideas
predominant relative to such matters. I allude to the fact to induce the brethren so
situated to deliberate on their surroundings, reflecting maturely on the future effect
which a reduction of their fees might produce. The cost of living is no higher here
than in most ohhe States in the Union, whilst our minimum fees and dues are double,
often treble, that of the ruling rates of other Grand Lodp:es. I have been connected
with :Masonry long enough to learn that the amount of fees for the degrees never
deters bad men from petitioning for admission, wnilst often, within my knowledge,
it has kept good men from applying for initiation to our Lodges.
I have granted dispensations to form six Lodges daring the term, all of them in
localities likely to conduce to the welfare of our Society. The progress made by
the new Lodges is highly commendable, pursuing a cautions and prosperous course,
with 11 prospect of becoming useful members of the brotherhood in this State. I
have discountenanced the proposed formation of two Lodges, when consulted by
those agitating the question, on account of proximity to new Lodges not as yet
tlrmly established. A sense of duty constrained me to decline issuing a dispensation
t6 form one Lodge, for several reasons. The unfortunate brother selected for Master
was totally blind, and otherwise physically maimed, therefore constitutionally dis·
qualified; whilst the statement that accompanied the petition did not refer to the
number of its inhabitants and the general resources of the vicinity, and the probable
permanency of the town; nor had the Master selected a certificate of capacity rrom
the Inspector of the Masonic district or Grand Lecturer, which our laws should
require, in addition to the usna.l one of some Master of a Lodge. There is an evident
propriety in requiring twelve members to sign the petition before granting a dispensation. Numbering as above, all the offices can be properly filled in a Lodge; with
but seven, it is impossible to fill the stations, or perform the work in either 11 creditable or impressive manner.

A fear of this Grand Lodge being desirous of centralizing too much power over
its subordinates, has been repeatedly expreaeed to me in conversation during the
past year. To snch an opinion my uniform reply was, that the provisions for the
subordinates-the component parts of the Grand Lodge-in the Constitution were
pla.in..and explicit. No one could or had complained ht my knowledge of the excess
-0f power wielded therein; whilst additions or amendments, supposed to affilct their
righta, conld only be admitted by their votes. It was, therefore, within their province, by their votes, to regnlate any tendency to a supposed nnnsoal nsnrpation of
power.

and equal jnstioe, and to snbserve only-the interest and honor of the Fraternity at

In presenting for your inspection 11 recapitulation of the quarter-centennial labors
of this Grand Lodge and of the correlative business transactions of the State for the same
period, and in rendering an account of my stewardship for the official year, I have
had, in the general retrospect, but one aim: the desire to promote the interests of
my brethern of this jurisdiction. With my most earnest efforts, I have attempted to
fulfill every function of 11 position most honorable to all who attain it; by so discharging the important duties devolving upon me as to merit your indulgent and fraternal approval, conscious that all persona may commit errors, I have endeavored
to the best of my ability to avoid them, wielding the high authority in me vested
with perfect impartiality, thereby promoting the welfare, prosperity, and happiness
of the entire brotherhood.
In conclusion, my thanks are due Rnd are most fraternally tendered to my colleagues the Grand Officers, especially those whom officially I have encountered most:

to respond most courteously to any demand made on their time, and for valuable
assistance in the discharge of my duties. I also with pleasure testify to the uniform
kindness and special attention shown me by the Inspectors, Officers, and Brethren
wherever convened in this jnrisdiction, and tender my renewed heartfelt thanks for
their kind brotherly receptions on all occasions.

At the Annual Communication in 1872 the action of fourteen Lodges, in cases of
trial, was reversed and eet aside, and the cases were remanded to the respective
Lodges with an order for further proceedings. At the following Communication, in
1873, six of those cases were properly accounted for by the Lodges; and, during this
year, three others have been re-tried and reported among the foregoing. But there
are still five other cases which, notwithstanding the twice repeated mandate of the
Grand Lodge, have been ignored or neglected by the Lodges to which they were
remanded, and it would seem to be quite time that the Grand Lodge should take
some action to insure obedience to its commands. These doubly delinquent cases
are as follows, viz., fromYolo,

The Grand Lecturer presented his Annual Report to the Grand
Lodge, as follows :To the M. •• W. •• Grand Lodge of OaJ:ifornia :

2,918 70

Amount carried forward,. ................................$13,508 73

In accordance with a regulation of the Grand Lodge, I herewith submit a report
of my official acts as Grand Lecturer during the past year.
Immediately after the 'anuoala*ctions in December last I commenced the
instruction of officers of dilierent ~ee who applied to me for that purpose, and
have since visited several of the Masonic districts and have examined the Inspectors
and instructed the officers of Lodges therein. In every instance· my reception and
ireatment were most kind and courteous and the suggestions offered were cheerfully
adopted.
Reports from all the Inspectors, excepting those of Districts Nos. 15 and 27, have
been received, which show a most satisfactory condition of the Lodges in the jnrfs.
diotion, both as to nniformity of ritual and the manner of keeping the records. From
these reports and my own observations I conclude tbat the present eyet.em of inspeotorehip, thongh not perhaps entirely satisfactory at first, has proven the most efficient
of any heretofore t.ried towards securing that perfect uniformity contemplated and
which is so ardently to be desired. Especially has the provision requiring the qualification of Masters elect before installation proved most satisfactory in the reealt
sought to be obtained; and the regulation should not only be continued, but its
requirements rigidly enforced.

[Oct. 13,

I ha.ve received no certificates either of installation or qualification of Masters
from the following Lodges: Nos. 8, 17, 27, 31, 33, 54, 76, 85, 100, 115, 122, 177, 218,
221, 223, and 224. In reference them, I can only presume that the requirements of
the Grand Lodge have been complied with. Proper returns from all the other
Lodges have been received.
In pursuance ofthe resolution passed a.t the la.st Annna.l Commnnication, a.nd by direction of the Grand Master, I notified the Inspectors of the severa.1 Masonic Districts to me.et
rue here a.t the Temple on the seventh day of the present month, for the correction of
errors, if any were to be fonnd, and to enable me to oa.rry into elfect the provision
of sa.id resolution in the exemplification of work before this Grand Lodge. I regret tba.t
so many were prevented, by business or other causes, from being present. Several,
however, were prompt in their attendance, a.nd I am Ratlsfted that much good has
resulted from such convention of Inspectors. Many dilferences were found to exist,
which, though not altogether serious, were yet sufficient to create confusion where
the strictest harmony should prevail. In this connection I wonld suggest, as the best
a.nd perhaps only remedy, tha.t a rigid Inspection and thorongh qualification of every
Inspector .hY the Grand Lecturer be required; and to this end, I would recommend
that the Grand Master appoint the several Inspectors before the close of the Grand
Lodge, and that each appointee be required to qna.lify himself thoroughly for the
responsible duties a.ssigned him at as early a period thereafter as possible. I would
further suggest that the Grand Lecturer and Inspectors be required to 8.!ISemble at
least twice ea.ch year for the purpose of correction and rehearsal of work.
All which is respectfully submitted by
THOMAS HUBBARD CASWELL,
Grand Lecturer.

ALABAMA.
The Grand Lodge of this State commenced its flfty·third Annual Communication
in the city of Montgomery, on the first day of December, 1873,-the M.·. W.·.
JOSEPH H. JOHNSON, Grand Master, presiding, and the R.·. W.". DANIEL SAYRE being
Grand Secretary. There were two hundred Lodges represented.
The Grand Master's Address is more a report of his official transactions than an
"address," in the general acceptation of that term, and its details abundantly show
that the office of Grand Master in Alabama is by no means a sinecure. Daring the
year he had been appealed to and had decided almost every conceivable question
that coald arise in Masonic usage or .Juriepruclence, and, what is more, enjoyed the
singular good fortnne to have all hie decisions and rulings indorsed by the Grand
Lodge as " eminently oorrect." The decisions generally are common sense rulings
in accordance with well-established law and usage; and, so far as we have been able
to discern, announce no new departures. One of the rnlings, however, has chaL
lenged oar special attention: "A dimit is not sufficient evidence that a man is ""
Mason. A petition for affiliation can be received before the applicant le examined,
bat the applican.t most have a voucher, or be examined, before he can sit in the
Lodge." ·
An applicant for affiliation, with us, mast come recommended by two brethren of
the Lodge, and we are at a loss to conceive how they conld recommend him unless
they were prepared to voachfor him as a Master Mason in good standing. We dissent
from onr eminent brother of Alabama on this one point, and hold that the Master of
a Lodge should not permit the reception of a petition for affiliation anleB8 the
brethren recommending the petition conld voach for him.

Bro. 'KNOTT distinguished himself as chairman of the Committee on Work and
on Foreign Correspondence. He was B genial companion, an enthusiastic Mason,

Memorial tablets were inserted in the printed proceedings to the memory of both

The Report on Correspondence is from the pen· of Bro.'KNOTT, and was his le.et
Masonic work. It comprises a review of the proceedings of twenty-seven Grand
Lodges. California Is not one of those reviewed, which fact we much regret. The

There are 395 Lodges in the jurisdiction, with a membership of 10,081. There
were initiated daring the year, 691 ; passed, 647; raised, 637; affiliated, 422; suspended for non-payment of dues, 634; reinstated, 1~7. There were, also, 24 expulsions and 26 suspensions for unmasonic conduct.
We notice that the Grand Lodge of Alabama publishes a list of all brethren
expelled and suspended, including those suspended for non-payment of does. While
we do not feel mach sympathy for a brother who can so violate the beneficent laws
of Masonry as to make it necessary .that he should be expelled from the rights and
privileges of the Lodge, we do have a sympathy for the brother who has been
suspended for non-payment of dnes .and whose claims on the FraterJJ.ity are not
thereby lost, bat only held in abeyance. We think that to publish hie suspension to
the world is not only nncharitable bat unjust. It is trae that oar Alabama brethren
also publish a list of restorations, bat that is poor amends for the wrong. The
brother suspended for non-payment of does may restore himself to good standing at
any time by paying hie does; yet the wound inflicted by the publication of his "bad
et.anding" still remains. Do what he may, the smirch on his Me.sonic character still
clings to him, and, like the blood of the murdered DUNCAN, will not "oat."

The Grand Lodge passed resolutions abolishing the penalty of suspension or expulsion for non-payment of dues, substitntina; tl\erefor " depriva.1 of membership,"
and providing that the brother " so excluded shall thereupon become non-affiliated."
He may be restored to membership ••by .a majority vote of the members present at
any stated communication of the Lodge, on the payment of all arrearages." A resolution was also passed requiring the Lodges to notify all non-affiliates that they
must apply for membership io some Lodge within six months, and providing that all
who fail to do so " shall be subject to such penalty as, after doe trial, the Lodge may
Impose." These two resolutions taken together, to oar mind, bear the appearance
of Jneonsistency. The first empowers the Lodge to make ·non-affiliates,. while the
second declares non-affiliation an offense . "subject to such penalty as, after doe trial, the Lodge may impose." The Grand Lodge also passed a resolution providing
that "non-affiliated Masons shall not be permitted to visit any of the subordinate
Lodges in this jurisdiction more than twice in a year!" We think tbat oar brethren
of Colorado have got the question of non-affiliation somewhat mixed, and that, If
they keep on In the same direction, they will soon require"the proverbial shrewdness
of \be "Philadelphia lawyer" to expound it.

The Grand Master's Address is an admirable paper, showing that he is not only
an ardent Mason but learned in Masonic literature. A large number of decisions
are reported, which are generally in harmony with well-established principles of
Masonic law and nsage. Some of them, however, a.re at variance with California
Ideas, bot they are doubtless in accordance with the law of bis jurisdiction, as the
Grand Lodge approved them all.
We offer no apology for making the following extract from this admirable address, and we commend its careful consideration to the craft of this jurisdiction:Tbe government of a Masonic Lodge partakes very largely of the patriarchal or
J&ternal. The first officer is called, with intelligent design, Master, indicative of bis
411t\hority and right to obedience; "Worshipful" as indicative of the reverence and
~apect which is due tci him. It is true that be is aoooally elected by the free choice
JI his brethren, but when elected and installed into his exalted station be bas the
ority Of a Father, and the members of bis Lodge are bis brethren; nay more
n that, they are his children and entitled to his sympathy, bis cooosel and his
ng admonition. How peantifolly the idea is expressed In the charge that he shall
be one to whom the burdened heart may poor out its an_goisb, distress may prefer
it1 snit, whose band is guided by justice and whose heart ls expanded by benevolence,
a hearty, earnest longing for the best good and continued well-being of the whole
hGman family, but more especially of the brethren, n. lover of harmony and concord,
a toother of strife, an encourager of the virtuous, a correcter of the evil, a living
every-day example In all the varied walks of life of the praotical embodiment of the

WHEREAS, At the last session of this Grand Lodge certain resolutions were adopted making the keP.ping of saloons b;r Masons in this jurisdiction a Maeonio oft'ense,

IOWA.
The Grand Lodge of this State commenced its thirty-first Annual Communication
in Des Moines, on the second day of June, 1874,-the M.'. W.·. JOSEPH CHAPKAN,
Grand Master, presiding, and the R.'. W.-. THEO. S. PARVIN being Grand Secretary.
Representatives from two hundred and thirty Lodges were present.
The Grand M88ter's Address is ao earnest and able document. He had reversed
the decision~ of several of his predecessors, and even " ignored a resolution of the
Grand Lodge to protect the individual Mason in his individual personal Masonic
rights." He says ... It is a consummation to he devoutly wished that Grand Lodges
in this country should learn that a M88on, he he Entered Apprentice, Fellow Craft,
or Master Mason, has rights of which he cannot he d,eprived withont a fair hearing
and the judgment of his brethren." He congratulates the Craft on the adjustment
of the difficulties heretofore existing between the Grand Lodges of Canada and
Quebec.
A regulation of the Grand Lodge requires the payment of a fe~ of three dollars for
a dispensation to ~confer the degrees out of time." This Bro. CHAPKAN objects to,
for two reasons: "lat, It interferes with the prerogative of the Grand Master; and
2d, It has the appearance of making merchandise, not only of the dispensing power,
but also of the applicant's nece•slties."
He says that dues are a modern invention, and, though he does not question the
right of a Lodge to discipline a hrnther for the non-payment of does, yet he doubts
its power " ~ cot him off from Masonic recognition and separate him as unworthy,
and make him as though_he · had never been a Mason." But the Most Worshipful
brother suggests no plan by which Lodges can be maintained without the levying of
does, and certainly the burden of their support should fall equally upon all members.
According to the law of oar Grand Lodge, a brother sll8pended for the non-payment of does can place himself in good standing by paying the amount of his
Indebtedness. This, certainly, is neither unjust nor severe. Does, we think, are
absolutely necessary to the support of the Lodge, and without some means of
enforcing their payment, many .of the brethren would be "drones in the hive."
Several decisions are reported, mainly touching oo well settled points, or being
of a local character ; hence we do not chronicle them.
Bro. PARVIN, the Grand Secretary, submitted an elaborate report of the business
of his office. Six dispen88tions for the formation of new Lodges had been issued
during the year. Bro. A. J. KELLOGG had been commissioned as Grand Representative near the Grand Lodge or South Cari;ilina, and a like honor had been conferred
upon our M.'. W.'. Grand Master, Bro. TITUB, who, we are told," was initiated,
years ago, in Cedar Lodge, No.11, at Tipton, Iowa."
Bro. PABVIN Is also Grand Librarian, and reports the addition of one hundred
and eighty volumes to the Grand Lodge Library during the year.
The reoelpts of the year amounted to Sll,013 76; and the disbursements were
Sll,112 64.

KAN BAB.
The eighteenth Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of Kansas was held
at Lawrence, commencing on the fifteenth day of October, 1873,-the M.-. W.-.
JOHN M. PBIOB, Grand Master, presiding, and the R ... w.·. JOHN H. BBOWN being
Grand Secretary. Seventy-one Lodges were represented.
The Grand Master's Address is characterized by good sense and a high moral
woe. It rt'presenta M88onry as in a healthy condition In the jurisdiction, but
expresses the fear that the Lodges are becoming too numerous. Doring the year he
bad granted dispensations for the formation of eighteen new Lodges, all which had
been put Into successful operation. He had made several decisions on points of
Jaw, a few of which we preaent:By a majority vote of lhe members present at a regular meeting, a Lodge can
make a reasonable assessment on its own members for charitable purposes or legit!·
mate Lodge expenses, bot not to assist in building a M88onic Hall. Funds for t he
latter purpose must be raised by voluntary oontribntions.
.
Lodges, while under dispensation, cannot affiliate Masons; cannot dimit its membero • cannot lay corner-stones of public bnilding-1·; cannot dedicate Masonic Halls;
oann~t recommend a petition for dispensation to form a new Lodge ; cannot give
permission to another Lo_dge to advance ~ ~rother; cannot tr,r one of its memb_e rs
for unmasonic comlnct; m fact, can only initiate, pass, and raise Masons, accordwg
to the express terms of their letters of dispensation.
When a brother received the first and second degrees in one Lodge, and, by its
request, the third degree was conferred in another, he becomes a member of the
Lodge conferring the third degree, on signing the By-Laws.
.
The Master and Wardens cannot resign or dimit during the term for which they
were elected and instal!ed.
In con9lnsion, Bro. BROWN makes the following eloquent remarks on the subject
of Masonic charity:Masonic Charity and relief are the fundamental principles of our Order, and we
lnoolcate and practice them 88 the tenets of our profession. "Faith may be lost In
sight, Hope end In fruition, but Charity ex~nds beyond the grave , throughout the
boundless 1·ealms of eternity." The potency, mfinenoe, and success of our noble Order
are mainly due to the silent ministrations of our munificent Charity. Masonry cannot
&tlbdue the tempest nor say to the ocean ••Peace, be still," bat it lifts the sinking
mariner from ·the engulling wave and warms him into life. It cannot hush the voice
of the thunder nor arrest the lightning's fiery missile, but it takes the victim of the
storm and wraps its snow-white robe around him. It does not stand at the door of
the sepulcher to roll away its stone and bid its silent, solemn tenant come forth, but
it finds the lame, the halt, and the blind, that have fallen by the way-side, and po~rs
into their hearts the oil of joy and gladness. It does not go abroad to proclaim 1ta
b11nevolent spirit, bot It wipe• the tear from the widow's eye and guides the feet and
guards the head of the orphan. It does not boast of its deeds of Charity, bot it'
"feeds the hungry, clothes the na~ed , and binds up t~e wounds _of th~ _amicte~." It
does not claim that it h88 fraterruzed the world, but it diffuses its spmt of umversal
Brotherhood and Charity 88 gentle as the dews of Hermon and a11 genial as the
light of Heaven.

KENTUCKY.

The seventy-fourth Annual Communicatlon of this Grand Lodge was commenced in
the city of Louisville, on the twenty-first day of October, 1873,-the M.-. W.-. EDWABD
w. TURNER, Grand Master, presiding, and the R.·. W.-. JoHN M. S. McCoRKLE being
Grand Secretary. There were four hundred and seven Lodges represented, and
eleven Past Grand Masters of the jurisdiction were present at the opening of the
session.
.
.
The Grand Master's Address is brief and mostly taken up with matters of a local
character. He alludes in glowing terms io the "Masonic Widows and Orphan.~
Home," at Louisville, which is represented as being in a prosperous conditi?n, furnishing a comfortable home for ninety-one beneficiaries-widows and orphans of
deceased brethren of the jurisdiction. From decisions reported we quote the following:· If a brother wishes to prevent the install~tio~ o.f a Master elect, he mus~ do so. at
the proper time and in the proper place, which 1~ m the Lodge "'.he~ the mstall1'!g
officer is about to install him in the Lodge, and his reasons for obJectmg must be m
writing and be valid ones.
The Grand Master bas no power to grant. a dispeus~tion to hol.d an election for
officers of a Lodge when it failed to hold 1t at the time prescribed by the Constitution; the same rule prevails if an election is held informally or should be illegal· in such cases the old officers hold over.
A dimitted worthy Master Mason, at his request, is entitled to be buried with
Masonie honors •
.A subordinate Lodge can not grant a dimit to any elective officer during the term
of said officer.
·
•
One of the Lodges had elected officers at the constitutional time, but when they
presented themselves for installation the Master refused to install them for two
reasons: first-because they were voted for by members who wefe disqualified to
vote by the by-laws of the Lodge, they being in arrears for dues; second, because
the officers elect were ineligible, they being in arrears for dues at the date of their
election. An appeal was made to the Grand Master, and he overruled the objections
and appointed a proxy to proceed with the installation. The Grand Master's proxy
attended at a regular meeting of the Lodge to carry out the instructiolli! of the Grand
Ma.ster, bat was met by an appeal from the Grand Master's decision to the Grand

18~4.]

Grand Lodge -of California.

507

Lodge, which he entertained, and declined to proceed with the installation. In
referring to this strange proced?re, the Grand Ma.ster say;:The Grand Master, in vacation, is the Grand Lodge, and his will is the supreme
Jaw and must be obeyed until the sitting of the Grand Lodge, to whom alone he is
amenable, and his decisions can not be rendered nail and void and of no effect by
an appeal. Whether the views entertained by us in this matter are correct or not,
we tee! that, by the non-installation of the officers elect, the prerogatives of the Grand
Mas~er have been invaded.
The matter was referred to a special committee whose report substantially sos·
tained the Grand Master. It held that the by·law of the Lodge was unconstitutional,
and that a member of a Lodge was eligible both to vote and hold office; notwithstanding his arrears for dues; that the only penalties known to Masonry are repri·
mand, suspension, and expulsion; and that" to debar a Mason of tile right to vote
or hold office, as the penalty for non-payment of dues, antagonizes a fundamental
principle of Masonic jU&tice."
The Grand Lodge ordered the Master of the Lodge to install the Master elect. It
also decided that" a brother can take an appeal from the decision of the Grand Ma'.
ter to the Grand Lodge, but, pending the time intervening the hearing of this appeal,
the.mandate of the Grand Master must be obeyed."
The Grand Lodge appropriated the sum of $500 for the relief of the brethren of
Memphis, Tennessee, and $250 for the relief of the brethren of Shreveport, Louisiana, then being ravaged by the ~holera.
The Grand Treasurer's report shows the receipts of the year to have been $30,059,

Master, had he en called to his rest; and EDWARD BARNETT, Past Deputy Grand Master
and Past Grand Secretary, had also been stricken down in the midst of a useful and

that they seemed in truth but one family, wherein no disoord could enter, much less

Under the by-laws of the Grand Lodge, if a sentence of suspension or expulsion
is overruled by the Grand Lodge, the brother can be restored to membership in his
Lodge only by unanimons ballot. The Grand Master thinks this law unjust. We
heartily agree with him, and think that the overruling of the decision of the Lodge
ought to place the brother in the same position which he before occupied in bis
Lodge.

The Master is, e:i: offl,cio, chairman of all committees, and the Lodge cannot restrict

An applicant for the degrees being elected, and allowing twelve months to expire
before presenting himself to receiv11 the same, must commence de nouo, the same as
on bis first application.
An applicant for affiliation must apply to the Lodge nearest his residence; and if
rejected, cannot apply to another Lodge without its consent.

A brother under charges is deprived of no privilege until found guilty.
It is not proper to allow Lodge rooms," dedicated to nniverMal bene volence and
Masonic purposes," to be nsed as ball rooms.
One who cannot write and sign Ilia name cannot be made a Mason.

We ofler no apology for making the following extract from the Address of the
Grand Master. The great number of ephemeral societies which are now being organized for ·a mushroom existence seem to call for some words of warning to our Craft
to restrain them from yielding to their blandishments, and we have rarely met with
more sensible remarks on the subject than tho&e of Grand M841ter NIOKERSON. After
alluding. to the imitations of Masonry by modern organizationi!, he says:It is certainly hij!'hly unbecoming and improper for a~y Mason to encourage or •
promote the adoption by any other organization of the peculiarities of Masonry.
They should be considered sacred. The ellect of these imitations is to lead the uninitiated to regard these associations as on an equality with our Institution, perhaps
co~ceding the latter to be a little older and more respectable. Some of these organi~at10ns nndoubtedly have worthy objects in view, but they follow Masonry at a long
mterval. They are modern, local, and short-lived, while Freemasonry is ancient,
universal, and immortal.
In this connection· I cannot refrain from condemning in the strongest terms the
transmitting of Masonic notices upon postaf cards and in unsealed envelopes; the
advertising .of Lodge meetings in the public prints, and especiall,)'. of the work to be
done at such meetings. Buch praotices are totally at variance with the time-honored
nsages and customs of the Fraternity, and can only tend to that familiarity which
· breeds contempt.
.
Nothing will more surely maintain the dignity and hiith importance of Masonry
than a return to the good old practices of the fathers, to guard with jealous care the
work of the Lodge and everything connected with it; to keep and conceal it from
the profane, absolutely; and to communicate it only to those of the Craft entitled to
know it, and to them only under proper circumstances, and with the most careful
restrictions; to avoid appearing in pnblic as Masons except upon strictly Masonic
oc~asions, and those of the highest importance, sanctioned by Jong usage ; nev"r to
write or print Masonic intelligence for the gratification of the curiosity of the profane , or the vanity of the initiated. We have wandered far from this high standard,
and the retnrn may be difficult; but I am convinced that the closer we confine Masonic
affairs to Masonic breasts, the better it will be for the Fraternity and its reputation.

Frequent applications have been made for dispensations to confer the degreea
upon the physically maimed and upon those who had not resided within our jurisdiction the required length of time; and, also, to confer all the degrees at one communication. All such applications have been unifol"tnly rPf•tsed-the first class,
becau•e I did notfeel at liberty to violate an ancient landmark; the second, because
I did not wish to establish the precedent of laying hands suddenly on any man ; and
the third, for tile rea~on that when men live for years in the vicinity of a Lodge and
do not feel a sufficient interest In, or love for, Masonry to apply for the degrees, and
only become alive to its beauty and advantages at the last moment, just as they are
upon the eve of takin~ some journey or emigrating to some other State, thAy can
hardly be said to be uni~uenced by mercenary motives, and, as a class, they ard
not such m~terial as we wish to work into our Mystic Temple.
Several 1Iecisions were made on questions of law and nsage, .all which were ratified by the Grand I,odge. As they announce no new doctrine and are m11stly on
points of a local nature, we do not deem it advisable to reproduce them.
The Grand Master deprecated non-affiliation. He thought that the affiliation fee
was responsible, in a great measure, for the evil, and recommended its abolishment.
The Grand Lodge adopted a resolution that "hereafter no fee shall be exacted for
the affiliation of a brother with any Lodge in this jurisdiction "-a step, in our
opinion, very decidedly in the right direction.
In concluding his address, Bro. GRISWOLD gives some excellent advice as to how
an "erring brother" should be treated. He says:We all, no doubt, would say that those who wantonly set aside the moral law,
who are not striving in some sense to "square their lives "by the·square of virtue,"
~honld not in the first rlace he admitted to our ranks; but what if we sometimes
find them already there or what if some brother, who for a time walked the path or
rectitude, under some severe temptation gives way and Is swept by the strong current into the whirlpool of vioe? What course shall we pursue then? As we see him
11radually swerving from the path of right, "will we whisper good counsel Into his
ear, and in too most tender manner remind him of bis faults, and endeavor to aid his
reformation?" or will we paBB him by In silence, shake oar heads suspiciously when
his name is mentioned, aud only Ray to others what we should say to him? As we
see him tottering to his final fall, will we stretch forth our hands to assist and support,
or only to give the final blow that shall hopelessly crash him to the ground? Shall
we with hearts of pity and compassion remember mercy, or shall we hasten to inflict
the e:x:tl'eme penalty of the law-to publicly disgrace him by summarily driving him
from our midst? Brethren, 1ohich of these couraes di1! we solemnly agree to pursue?
I need not wait your answer.
My observation teaohes me that those who are most lax in their views with reference to who should be admitted to our mysteries, who would open the door of the
lodge-room the widest to any who may wish to enter, are usually the first to urge
har•h measures in the treatment of the erring, to turn upon a falling brother and by
their merciless contempt to hasten him to hie final ruin. If we would only watch in
our brethren the very beginnings of vice, and when they are only in the outer circles
of the maelstrom hasten to give them "due and timely notice that they might ward
off all approaching danger," bow many might we thus save who otherwise wlll soon
be hopelessly engnlphed; how many might thus be kept from falling altogether. A.
member of a certain Lodge had become an incorrigible drunkard. Charges were
preferred against him; he was tried and expelled. As, after his expulsion, he
walked out of the Lodge into the Tyler's room, he said to the brethren," Well, boys,
If I had only received half as much good advice when I was learning to drink whisky
as loo have given me to-night, I might have been a different man." Brethren, if the
pomt of this sad story belongs to any of us let there be no hesitation In receiving it.
There will come a period in· the history of most Lodges when extreme measures mDBt
and should be used; then, let there be no hesitation in the rrompt and faithful
administration of justice. But this time should never come unti every other honor.able expedient has been frequently and persistently tried, but to no purpose.

MISSISSIPPI.
The Grund Lodge of Mississippi.held its fifty-sixth Annual Communication at
Canton, commencing on the third day of February, 1874,-the M.-. W.·. R. P. BowKN,
Grand Master, presiding, and the R.·. W.·. J. L. PoWER being Grand Secretary.
The Grand Master's Address is quite lengthy, but is chiefly devoted to local matters.
He had contributed one hundred and fifty dollars of the Grand Lodge fonds to the
relief ttf the Craft at Memphis, one hundred ·to the Orphan's Home at Lauderdale, and
smaller sums to other charitable purpos~s ; all which the Grand Lodge approved.
Bro. BowKN is a little sharp on those brethren who fail to pay their Lodge dues.
He had Issued an edict directing Masters of Lodges to enforce the by·laws In that
regard, and found .that much good had been done thereby "in the way of reinstate·
ment of members who had, from neglect, permitted themselves to fall behind with
their does." He says :Brethren, none should evade so sacred a responsibility, and if we have on our roll
Masons who so far forget themselves as to do so, all that we can do or ought to do Is
to strike them from the roll, suspend them, and if necessary expel them. We do not
need, we do not want, and we will not have such men in our Order. They are drones
in the great Masonic hive. Let. the more indns~rious. bees sting t?em hence. They
are Masons at our Annual Festivals, and on all ·pnbhc demonstrations are the first to
fall into line , thus proclaiming to the world, like the Pharisees of old, that they a.re
better thati others; but when thb more onerous duties incident to our calling require
their presence and aid, they all, with one accord, begin to make excuse. Throw
them overboard-lighten the ship.
He had issued seven dispensations for the formation of new Lodges during the
year, to six of which the Grand Lodge granted charters, continning the seventh
under dispensation. The Grand Lodge also granted dispensations for the formation
of three new Lodges. Several decisions were reported by the Grand Master, none of
which, however, are of general importance.
The Grand Secretary's report tells ns that the "financial operations of the Grand
Lodge seem now to be adjusted upon self-snsta.ining principles, and, with average
expenditures, the receipts will add a small balance annually to the Grand Lodge
treasury." We learn from the same source that seventy-eight Lodges are in arrears
for " annual returns, ledger balances, or annual dues." This is rather a bad showing, but it most be remembered that Mississippi has not had time yet to folly recover
from the devastations of the war, and that Masanry, through its disciples, snlfered
from its baneful effects with all other interests. We indulge the hope that the lapse
of a few more years will fiud the State prosperous and the Grand Lodge flourishing
with all its former vigor.
A proposition to amend the Constitution so as to anthorize the Grand Lodge. to
fix permanently the place of holding the "Annual Grand Commnnication," failed to
receive the constitutional majority and was lost. The vote stood-yeas, four hundred and twenty-three : nays, three hundred and forty-two. The next Annual Communication will be held at Meridian, on the second Monday in February, 1875.
The question as to whether it is proper to occupy halls jointly with other societies was referred to a committee. The majority reported, in substance, that
"Lodges may allow the use of their halls to any orderly body, the objects of whose
meetings are lawful and laudable, and not opposed to or antagonistic with the
principles of our institution." The minority reported that to do so" was nnmasonlc
and contrary to t·he spirit and genius of oar Order." The Grand Lodge adopted th
majority report.

MISS OURI.
The Grand Lodge of Missouri commenced its fifty-third Annual Communication in
Saint Louis, on the fourteenth day of October, 1873,-the M.·. w.-. SAMUEL H. OWENS,
Grand Maeter, in the chair, and the R.-. w.-. GEOBGK F. GoULEY being Grand Secretary. There were two hundred and thirty-four Lodges represented.
The Grand Master's Address is an unpretentious but sensible paper, mostly
occupied by the details of his olficial transactions. He announces the death of two
Past Grand Masters, Bros. WILLIAM D. Mum and JOHN F. RYLAND, to both of whom
he pays the tribute of high praise for the possession of many virtues as men and
Masons. He had been called upon to make numerous decisions on points of Masonic
Jaw and usage, thirty-one of which are reported for the consideration of the Grand
Lodge. Many of these are on well settled points of the" common law'' of the Craft,
while others are of a purely local character. We notice a few of those having a
general bearing :A Lodge had performed the funeral service over the grave of a brother "months
after his burial." The Grand Master decided that it was not only wrong but ridiculous and calculated to bring the Craft into contempt.
A member in good standing ·with his Lodge removed to California. He became
sick , after his arrival in California, was in indigent circumstances, and the Lodge
In whose jurisdiction he resided relieved his necessities, and when he died buried
him. It sent the bill of expenses to the Lodge of which he was a member, and the
Grand Master, being appealed to, decided that it was in duty bound to reimburse the
California Lodge.

We all know that no magnificence of architllctnre can give immortality, or even
length of years, to this building ol" ours. Without its beanteous walls, by wayward·
ness and wickedness of life, by forgetfulness of the precepts of Masonry, can we

our methods of life, rest assured that while these walls stand they will reproach ns'
•nd when they fall none will know why they were reared.
This edifice can be painf~ll;i: II!&rrell, for all purposes f?r which it was reared, by
:ronr lapses from duty. If, w1thm its walls, yon would realize calmness of conscience
and qnietness of life, if yon hope for harmony at yonr convocations, and kindly and
Civilizing and refining influences to go forth from it to all the fraternity, and to the
entire community In which it is so prond an ornament, on the part of this brotherhood
there must be uprightnP.ss of heart and life, and within iii and without it, seen and
unseen, each member mast cast aside trifling, and labor to maintain that cheerful
Integrity which Is itself virtue-which is itself Masonry.
Thus living, this oar temple-now forever consecrated and dedicated to Free.
masonry, to virtue, and to nniversal benevolence-shall be an unfailing fountain from
whence shall flow all the sweet charities of life and &II the holy ministries of love.

The Grand Lodge of Nebraska commenced its sixteenth Annual Communication

W." WILLIAM R. BOWEN being Grand
HILL, Grand Master, presiding, and the

The Grand Master's Address is brief and devoted exclnsively to the considera·
tion or affairs in his own jurisdiction. He had issued eight dispensations for the estab·
lishment of ::ew Lodges daring the year, and fonr for the conferring of degrees" oat
of the nsu11l time.'' At the preceding Annual Communication a rule had been
adopted requiring a fee of ten dollars for the latter class of dispensations, which, the
Grand Master says, "seeJDs to have materially diminished the emergent cases.
That Is, the most of cases are not so emergent when they cost ten dollars.'' He
recommends the continuance of the rule. He had made no decisions on questions
of law or usage of sufficient importance to be reported; bot had issued a clrcnlar
to the Lodges warning them against giving the aid of Masonry, In organized or
individual form, to a" Grand Gift Concert,", advertised at Omaha, for the purpose
of aiding I~ the erection of a Masonic Temple-the Grand Lodge, at its preceding
Annual Co10municatlon, having resolved that to do so was "nnmasonic and de·
sel'ving or reproof and discipline."
Non-affiliated Masons occupied considerable attention at the hands of the Grand
Lodge. A brother presented a long string of whereases and resolutions concerning
them, which, being boiled down, was to the effect that It was the duty of every
Mason to be a member of a Lodge, and that.non-affiliation was a "crime uf. magnl·
tnde that shonld call forth the severest discipline." The discipline proposed was
sospenslon or expulsion. The same brother offered a resolution providing 'that no
dimit shonld be granted to a ,brother, except on his written application, setting forth
that he desired the same for the sole purpose of affiliating with another Lodge ;
that the membership of the brother seeking a dimit should not cease in the Lodge
until it should have been' officjally notified of his election. to membership in another
Lodge; and that the dimit should become null and void if thP. brother failed to apply
for membership in another .Lodge before the expiration of ninety days. The resoln·
tions were referred to the Committee on J nrisprudence, who made the following
report, which was adopted:'
That, while we deprecate the growing tendency to non-affiliation, your committee
are of the opinion that a compulsory method of keeping Masons within the Lodge,
after they have once been made, is repugnant to the voluntary character of ·the
institution.
.
Your com10ittee are of the opinion that it Is unwise on the part of any Lodge to
refuse an application for a-dimit, on the part of a member in good standing, ~de.in
legal form and in good faith.
·
Your committee believe that, although dimlssion made with the intention of a total
disseverance from the Fraternity is a violation of Masonic duty, yet ·tJiere is no
power in a Lodge to refnse to act upon an application for a dimit when legally
demanded.

The Grand Master's Address is an admirable docnment-dignifled, but nnostentatioas, conched in purest English, without any attempt at display, it impresses the
mind of the reader that its author is not only a man of superior intellect but of
pure heart. He alludes in appropriate terms to tiie d·e ath of prominent Masons of
other jurlsdictione-OBB and BRUNS, of South Carolina; STEVENSON, of Virginia ;

Lodge of Engl11nd in the Bahamas. Of the death of the latter he says:The circumstances attending the death and burial of R .·. w.·. NA.THANIEL FRENCH,
Pro\fincial Grand Magter of the Grand Lodge of England in the Bahamas, were very
sad and painful ; and as they are so generally known I will not refer to them at
length. On his arrival in the city of New York it appears that he mnst have been
waylaid anJ drugged, in which condition he was taken to a hospital, in a deranged
condition of mind from which he never recovered. After his death, and in the chi&f
city of this great Republic, his body was thrown with six hundred others into a pit,
where decomposition rendered it impossible to recognize it, when sought for to
accord him Masonic and decent burial. The klnd offices ol' his brethren, in the loves·
ti11ation of hie death and burial, occasioned so much inquiry as will probably lead to
a reform In the practice of burying the poor and unknown dead in such an mhoman
and dishonorable manner.

Grand Lodge of California.

527

of the Lodgee, requesting him to call an Emergent Communication of the Grand
J,odge to take action in regard to the alleged cruel and inhuman treatment to w}lich
Masons and their widows end orphans were subjected in the island of Cuba by the
Spanish authorities and their dependents. This the Grand Mester declined to do for
the following reasons:The account of the reported butcheries and outrages was improbable on its face;
there was no reliable testimony to establish its truth, and ft was wholly discredited.
At the same time the people of this country were in a state of feverish anxiety at the
prospect of war with Spam, consequent upon the treatment to which the crew of the
Virgmius were Rnbjected on their capture in Spanish waters, and a saspicion was
entertained that an attempt was beiniz: made to use the Fraternity as a means of
strengthening the popular excitement in favor of the prosecution of hostilities against
Spain, on the part of this conntry, for the benefit of the Cnbans.
If the story of their wrongs, in all the details as presented, was true, the Masons
of Cuba and their families were entitled to our sympathies and our fraternal assist·
ance; but the Grand Lodge could do nothing to aid them in their extremity, by
holding an emergent communication to consider their condition; bot, on the con·
trary, such a course would rather add to their misery. if that were possible, by
drawing the attention of their persecutors to the fact that Masons elsewhere were
seeking to arouse the indignation and torn the civilized world against them-which
would inevitably result to the disadvantage of those whom it was desired to assist.
If It was designed by the movement to ose the Fraternity in shaping the political
aspect of .the question of a war with Spain, it was equally improper to convene the
Grand Lodge-for Masonry cannot legitimately be employed for any such purpose.
Brn. Fox le not in favor of permitting balls dedicated to Masonry to be occupied
by other societies. In referring to this matter, he says-The re,pid Increase of ephemeral societies during the past few years has occasioned
a demand in me,oy localities for the use of Masonic apartments for their meetings.
During the past year frequent applications were made in behalf of Lodges for permiBBioo to rent their rooms to other associations ; and, while not refusing permission,
t>xcept in cases where Lodge rooms had been solemnly dedicated, I could only reply
that the Grand Lodiz:e had no regulation on the subject, probably for the reason that
it contemplated no such employment for Masonio apartments, and that a Lodge ought
to have a sufficient degree of pride in its connection with onr ancient and honored
Fraternity to 1·efuse, for .the sake of the few dollars it would gain, to allow the nee of
its rooms for any bot Masonic purposes. Moch contention and ill feeling has grown
out of the practice, and it is recommended that a regulation on the subject be pro·
posed for incorporation in the Statutes, so that in future Lodges may act and govern
themselves accordingly.

The effect of this clause is to enable one to withdraw who has ceased to desiYe

He by no means thereby absolved himself from those obligations wuich are permanently chargeable, even on bis expulsion. Re has waived a benefit, but remains
snbject to those duties which are of life-long obligation.
We are aware that the remedy given by the New York Code is deemed by some
too sharp and decisive, but all such should ree:d the able and convincing argument of

if he had a limb that was attaclied with gangrene, from which death would soon and

to save It, a limb, even all of them, would be sacrificed, for mercy to the criminal is

OHIO.

The Grand Lodge of Ohio held its slxty·foorth Annual Communication in Columbos, commencing on the twenty-first day of October, 1873,-the M.·. W.·. ASA H.

The Grand Master's .Address fills sixteen closely printed pages. During the year

the regulations. He had received many appl,ications for dispensations authorbiing
Lodges to appear in procession upbu "Decoration Day" and the Fonrth of July, al
which he had refused, believing that" no Masonic procession should be permitted
except on occasions pnrely Masonic.'' · He had written more than two thousand
letters during the year in response to those received from members of the Craft, and
had decided many questions of Masonic jurisprudence. He reports only one deci •
sion: There was a regnlarly constituted Lodge in the village of Comminsville; the
village was annexed to the city of Cincinnati ; and the question was asked the Grand
Master "whether, by reason of the annexation of the village to the eity, by which it
became a part thereof, the jurisdiction of the Lodge was changed or atfected?"
The Grand Master decided in the negative, as follows :-'When a Lodge, duly chartered and constituted, located in an incorporated village,
and such village afterwards, by action of the prop~r civil authorities, becomes
annexed to and constitutes a part of a citt, such annexation does not in any manner
atfect the territorial jurisdiction of the cdp;e. I admit that considerable may be
said upon both sides of this questiou; bot it aeeJ.Ds to me that, when the territorial
jurisdiction of a Lodge is fixed and defined by· the action of this Graud Body,
nothing but its action can in any mauner alter or change.it.

The Grand Master's Address is an able and earnest document, showmg that he is
imbued with th~ true spirit of Masonry and is a zealous worker for 'the advancement

thereof. The brethren of Oregon, like those of California, hail from every quarter
of the Masonic world and have broµght with them the work of their mother Lodges.
The natural consequence of this is a confusion of work-a kind of hodge-podge made
np of the recollections of the Master, and liable to be materially changed with each
change of Master. Old brethren of California have a lively recollection of the same
~late of atfuirs in this jorlsdict.lon. The writer of this was first instructed in the
work by a very" bright " brother from Ohio ; but another " bright " brother, ha~ling
from Illinois affiliated with the Lodge and was elected Master. The latter materially
changed the' work, and under his Instructions we got the ritnal so thoroughly mixed

QUEBEC.
The fourth Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of Quebec was commenced
in the city of Montreal, on the twenty-fourth day of September, 1873,-the M. •• W.·.

534

Proce,edings of the

J. H. GRAHAM, Grand Master, presiding, and the R.·. W.·. J. H. ISAACSON being
Grand Secretary. Thirty-eight Lodges were represented.
The Grand Master's Address is mostly occnpied with the consideration of local
affairs. Thirty-six Grand Bodies had recognized the Grand Lodge of Que bee " as the
only rightful Sovereign Masonic authority in and for the province of Quebec." The
Grand Lodge of Canada persisted in violating the jurisdictional rights of Quebec, and
had rejected overtures made for reconciliation and settlement of the differences
existing between the two Grand Bodies.
The Grand Master also complains of the existence of "Private Lodges" within
his jurisdiction, working under authority of the Grand Lodges of England and Scot
land. The Grand Master of England claims that this is in accordance with an agreement entered into between the Grand Lodges of England arrd Canada, prior to the
organization of the Grand Lodge of Quebec, and consequently not an invasion of
~he·rights of the latter. To this Bro. GRAHAM replies that such an arrangement" is
contrary to the well established principle of Grand Lodge Sovereignty, injurious to
the interests of the Craft, and of no binding force on the Grand- Lodge of Quebec."
The Granll Master had issued one dispensation for the formation of a new Lodge
daring the year, and had refused to issue a dispensation for the formation of a Lodge
within the Jnriadiction of the Grand Lodge of Canada, thus declining to resort to
retaliation.
The receipts of the year amounted to $1402 39, anll the 1disbursements were
$1603 74.

laudable efforts for human improvement and reform: your principles and pledges
will ever prompt yon to. this, and will, I trust, not be disregarded. And above all,
let us look well to oar own ways, studying ever, by the judicious use of the GatJel,
to break off all the excrescence• of our frail, human character, and preparing our. selves, by the aid of the Great Architect of the Universe, to take our place as polished
forever presides, forever reigns. And let
stones in the Eternal Temple, where

us strive faithfnlly, earnestly, manfully, to do our appointed work, and we shall not

TEXAS.
The proceedings of the Grand Lodge of Texas come to us in a neatly printed
volume of three hundred and thirty-six pages. The thirty-eighth Annual Communi·
cation was held in the city of Hocrston, commencing on the third day of June, 1874,
-the M.·. w.·. JAMliS F. MILLER, Grand Master, presiding, and the R.·. W.·. GROROE
H. BRINGHURST being Grand Secretary. The representatives of one hundred and
twenty Lodges were present at the commencement of the session.
The Grand Master's Address is a well writt~n paper, full of noble sentiments. He
represents the Craft in Texas as enjoying a higher degree of prosperity than at any
. previous time since the organization of the Grand Lodge, but is apprehensive that
this prosperity itself may lead to injury through the too r11.pid multiplication of
Lodges and the consequent introduction of improper material. He says:There is a tendency to multiply the number of Lodges to sn•h an extent that we
will soon have, in some portions of the State, a great many weak and poor Lodges,
unable to discharge their duties to the Order 01· to the Grand Lodge. At every
cross-roads and school-house there is a disposition to organize a Masonic Lodge as
a matter of convenience and as an inducement to immigrants, so t!{at in many CO!lJl·
ties there are now t'rom five to ten Masonic Lodges. These Lodges, of course, must
each have a Ma•onic hall, furniture, etc., at a pretty heavy cost. This will be a great
temptation to work unworthy material ih their spiritual temple,in order to strengthen
themselves and pay off their indebtedness. It is true that the very heavy immigration
to our State has so far, in a great measure, counteracted this evil, but it is time that
precautionary measures were taken. Another source of some trouble, which may
some day bring trouble upon us, i; the opinion that is taught and believed in some
quarters, that because a man is a good citizen and no harm is known of him, when
he petitions a Lodge he has aright to the degrees, and that it is an outrage to reject
him. It seems to me, however, that the very reverse of all this should be taught and
enforced. No man has any right or interest in this Order. except its members, o.ud
if the admission into it of the must distiuguished citizen in the land would disturb the
good fellowship of the 'humblest member of the l..odge, his petition should be rejected,
During the year the Grand Master had issued nineteen dispensations for the form·
ation of new Lodges, had refused thirty-one applications therefor, and had referred
four others to the Grand Lodge. This looks to us like a "tendency to multiply
Lodges," and would appear to justify the fear expr~sed by Bro. MILLER. But
Texas has a vast territory and her population is rapidly increasing, which may
render necessary this apparently too rapid increase of Lodges.
During the year the Grand Master had been called upon to decide about two
thousand questions upon Masonic jurisprudencj\, usage, or ritual! He reports forty·
two of his decisions to the- Grand Lodge, portion of which we sti°bjoin :A Lodge cannot confer the degrees on a candidate, previously rejected by another
Lodge, without its consent. Neither lapse of time, distance, nor removal from one
jurisdiction to another can be held under our regulations to defeat the jurisdiotion
acquired by regular petition and ballot.
When a Mason dies, being at the time.under suspension for non-payment of dues,
his family cannot, after his death, pay up his does and the-reby restore themselves to
such Masonic privile!Jes as they would have had if he had died in good standing iu
the Lodge. A Mason s family can have no Masonic privilege except through the
Mason himself: after his death his status towards the Order can not be changed by
any act of theirs.
After a Lodge receives a petition for degrees it must be balloted upon, unless it
appear that the Lodge bas no jurisdiction in the premises, or that the petitioner is
physically disqualified. The report of the Committee on Character cannot dispense
with the necessity for the ballot.
A Mason cannot lawfully avouch for another unless he has sat in open Lodge
with him, and his recollection of the fact should be so distinct as to enable him to
point out time and place with certainty. Anti..Jurther, a brother cannot lawfully
avouch for ·another upon the 11vouchment of another brother who has sat in Lodge
wit)) the visitor, but was not'able to be present, nor·can it be done upon any private
examination.
A.candidate who had lost the forefinger of the left hand (or any finger) has not
the physical qualifications for the degrees required by our regulations.

Under the regulations of the Grand Lodge of Texas a brother may sign a petition
for a dispensation for a new Lodge while a member of a chartered Lodge; but when
the ~w Lodge receives its charter, he then, ip8o facto, ceases to be a member of the
old Lodge. Our regulations require that the dimit of' each petitioner for such a dispensation shall accompany the petition. This, we think, is the better plan, as all
the members of the new Lodge can start in to build it up without liability for dues
or assessments elsewhere.
The Grand Master recommended the holding of "a Lodge of Sorrow" annnalh·
during the session of the Grand Lodge, and it was so ordered. A committee w~~
appointed to make the necessary arrangement3 for holding one at the ~ext Annual
Communication.
A Committee was appointed to consider and report upon the JH'acti~ability of
establishing a "Masonic Agricnltnral and Mechanical School" for the education of
Master Masons' orphans, to report at the next Annual Communication.
The Committee on Masonic Jurisprudence reported adversely on the renting of
Lodge rooms to other than Masonic bodies. The Grand Lodge adopted the report;
and so hereafter, in Texas, halls dedicated f.o Masonry will not be profaned by the
practice of other mysteries.
The same committee reported that the "fact of a Mason pleading 'limitation' in
bar of a snit, is not of itself evidence of wrongful intention nor of nnmasonic conduct." This was also approved by the Grand Lodge. We donbt the soundness of
his decision as a matter of morality. A brother taking advantage of another's hav·
ing indulged him by waiting, until the statute of limitations intervenes, for the payment .of moneys justly due, is certainly guilty of moral delinquency when he takes
advantage thereof to escape payment. A.II the sophistries of the most expert
pleaders cannot convince one's conscience to the contrary.

objection of a member of his Lodge to the admission of a visitor, the reason being
assigned and considered insufficient, Bro. CusmNa says: "We doubt the propriety
of driving out a member to admit a visitor. Hospitality is a good thing, but not to
be commended when it necessitates turning the children out of doors."

§§ 186-189. Treat on balloting for candidates. If one-third of the ballots cast
are black, the candidate is rejected for three years. If, after three years, he renews
his application and again receives one·third black balls, he stands rejected forever.
If three or more black ·balls appear, and if the number of black halls does not
a1Dount to one-third of the ballots cast·, the Master of the Lodge shall request the
breth"r en who have cast the black balls to state to him their reasons, in from three
to nine days. If they fail to do so during that time, no fnrther notice is taken of the
black balls cast. If the objections are made known within that time, they are laid
before the Lodge. If a majority of the members then vote for the candidate, and
the minority does not oppose it, tile candidate may be initiated. If the minority,
however, oppose the majority, the officers ot' the Lodge shall obtain the decision of
the Union Directory, before the candidate is initiated. If previous to balloting no
objections are raised, and two black bRlls appear, it may be assumed that a mistake
has occurred, and the ballot shall be declared clear.
§ 197. Every brother, who desires to affiliate with one of the daughter Lodges,
mnst be of the Christian faith, etc.
§ 206. Affiliation of brethren belonging to our Union is without fee .
§ 207. Entered Apprentices shall serve one year, and Fellow Crafts two years
before advancemen~.
§ 223. A Master l!hson, who is a member of a lodge affiliated with the Grand
Lodge Three Globu, may participate in balloting for candidates in other daughter
lodges.
'f he Lodge .Akazia, or .daughter Lodge of the Grand Orient of the Netherlands,
addressed the Grand Lodge Three Globes, proposing a mutual and firm alliance of
all Grand Lodges and Grand Orients, to be governed somewhat after the manner of
the Order of Jesuits. The formation of a Central Orient is suggested, where every
Grand Lodge or Graud Orient is represented by two delegates. This convention is
to elect one of their own members General Grand Master, aad its edicts shall be
biuding upon all Grand Lodges and Grand Orienta.
We allude to this proposition, because a somewhat similar plan has been broach·
ed by a German Lodge, to which we refer in another part of this Re port. We look
upon these propositions as evidence that the centralization of political power which
has made Germany a unit within the last few y ears, seems not to have remained without io6uence upon the Masonic mind of that country. But, as the realization of this
idea is, for the present, at least, decidedly improbable, sp eculations upon that subject would be useless. The Grand Lodge unanimously declared itself opposed to the
proposition, regarding it injudicious and impracticable, viewed even from an ethical
and pecuniary standpoint.

Your committee have given the subject a v&y careful r~xammation and can. see
no good reason for modifying the report made in 1863. Bearce a year has pa.seed smce

to the Grand Lodge in some form. Some of the brethren dislike the law which provides susnension a.a the penalty for neglect of the payment of dues, and, from time to
time, cas~ have been reported to us of hardships and seeming injustice; and we hav~
been urged to modify the rule prescribed by Bee. 11, Art.•m, Part ill, of the Constitution, in such wise a.s to allow Lodges to remit, or friends to pay, tbe ~ues of Maaons
who have died under suspension for that cause, and thus allow thell' names to .be
placed again upon the roll of the Lodge and permit the Lodge to bury them ~th
Masonic honors.
The Committees on Jurisprudence 'h ave ateadily opposed such modification, and
the present committee fully agrees in that with its predecessors. It is th~ duty of
every Lodge of Ma.sons and of its officers and members to see that no one 9f its ~em­
bers is wrongfully suspended for any cause. The Lodge is a family, an~, theore~cally
at lOOBt, every member is supposed to know and to feel a personaJ. mterest m ti:ie
welfare of ev&y other. The law requires that every member pay to his Lodge cer~
dues and directs that, in case of his neglect so to do for six months, he shall be notified by the Secretary of the fa.ct of hia delinquency ·and that he will be euspen~ed
unless he pay or show cause why he does not; and commands that in case, af~r notice,
he neglect to pay or show cause why he does not, the Master shall declare his e!18pe~­
aion 118 the judgment of the law. He must be notified of hie delinquency, and, if he lB
unable to pay, some one of the members of his Lodge ought to kn~w the fa.ct and
report it to the Lodge, when. his dues should be remitted or f~rther time be ~ranf:6d
for payment; and if there is no one who does know, some,one ought to mqu~e
and inform himself and hie Lodge, and no Master ought to declare any member bf~
Lodge suspended for non-payment of his dues unless he is e&tisfied that proper notice
ha.s been given and that the delinquent has the ability, but wilfully ~egl6'.'ts to perforn:
hie duty and deserves suspension. H proper care were taken m this regard, w
.
hould hear no tales of hardship or injustice in this connection.
s H orie wilfully negloots the performance of his duties he ought to be purus_he4 for
it· and if suspension is the proper punishment he ought to be suspended; an~ if death
o~e~take him while suspended for that cause, a.a for any other, the e~pens1on ought
to continue. He might in hie life-time have removed the cause, but did no: care to do
it, and it is a sickly sentimentality that fuduces us, simply ~use h~ 18. ~ead, to
mourn over him and to desire to show our mourning to th~ world. ~e h;ing. we
willing to let him remain suspended-would not pay his dues to r eheve him-and

to put ourselves to special inconvenience to manufactur.e good things to e&y. . .
Our business is. first of all with the living members-to look ofter them m s1~to tand by them in misfortune-to be friends to them in. adversity as well a.a m

It is, doubtless, true that injustice ha.s been eometim~ done by hasty and ~ad~
vised action under the section of our law which provides for eucJ;i suepene1Qns ,
but such injustice comes chiefly from the fa.ct that Masters have misconstrued the
law and have declared suspensions without any evidence that the party had bee_n
notlled of his delinquency. We take it to be a well recognized principle of Masomc
Jaw that no Illan can be deprived of hie rights and privileges, or be declared to have

:i :;

1874.]

Grand Lodge of OaJA,jornia.

561

been so deprived, without having had at lOOBt an opportunity to be heard in hie
defense. If he is contumacious and refuses to appear, after notice, judgment will
p888 against him by default. He haa had his opportunity to be heard. The proceedings under Bee. 11, Art. ill, Pe.rt ill, of our Constitution, e.re in the nature of criminal 'Proceedings ; but they are legal proceedings and constitute a trial. The charges
e.re that the party ha.a wilfully neglected hie duty to hie Lodge, in failing to pay in
to the treasury his just proportion of the funds necee'e&ry for its maintenance and
the performance of its legitimate work. He must be notified of the fa.ct that such
charge stands ~t him and must be answered; and the evidence must first show
that he ha.a been notified, else the Ma.star ha.s no jurisdiction to declare the judgment
cir the l&w, and the law itself declares no judgment-can declare no judgment.
It is not consistent with that higher law which is recognized in all but the most
despotic governments, that any one should be deprived of life, liberty, privileges, or
property without his day to be heard in defense. The Constitutions of all our States,
and of the United States, recogni7.e and declare the doctrine; and the courts of England have always held it to be the inalienable right of every Englishman and a right
which no law of Parliament could take away or abridge. We, a.a Ma.sons, could not
aff'ord to place ourselves on a level with the despotic governments of nations not yet
emerged from barbarism. Our government may be despotic, but it is the despotism
of enlightened, reasonable men, who regard and protect the rights of a.11.
Our law has never made any provision for notification to delinquents ·for nonpayment of dues, other than that provided for in the section before mentioned, which
is simply "that he eha.ll be notified by the Secretary that," etc. This, in our judgment, means persona.I service of the notice. An amendment of the definition of
"notification" was prepared la.at year, and will come up for final action at this Communication, which proposes that notifications .. eha.11, when practicable, be persona.lly
served upon the brother to be notified by a Tyler or some other Mason properly
deput.ed for the purpose. If this cannot be conveniently done, it shall be left at the
residence or usual pla.ce of business of such brother, or, if :ruch rellidence or place of
ln,£8iness is distant or unlcnown, it may be placed in the Poai--ojfiu, addressed to him
at M,s {ast known place of residence, and this shall be deemed due and l!Ujficient

aervice."
The kind of service proposed by the last clause of this proposed amendment will
answer very well and is unobjectionable for all ordinary notifications, but the notification ca.lled for by Bee. 11, Art. ill, Pe.rt m, is in effect a summons. It is an imperative order t.O show cause why he should not be adjudged guilty of a Masonic offense
and deprived of all his rights as a Mason. As we have. said, we do not think that it
is within the legitimate authority of this Grand Lodge, or of any Ma.sonic power, to
deprive a Maaon of his rights without due process of law, and that due proceee. of law
implies of necessity that the defendant have notice of his offense and have an opportunity to be heard in hie defense. Our law ought to provide for service of summons
in cases where the party to be served cannot be found, but such service must be reasonable, and should be made in such way as will be most likely to advise the defendant
of the pr~gs against him, and should allow him a re11Sonable time to appear
and defend. Delinquency for six months in the payment of dues is not so heinous
an offense that we should abandon all the decent forms of procedure and deal with
the party summarily.
In the case of Bro. l'EBEZ SNELL, reported by Bro. HILL, at page 84 of the
proceedings of 1873, the Grand Lodge of Louisiana had declared him expelled
because, in the bitter strife at that time (1841) existing between two bodies of the
Scottish Rit.&-the so-called Supreme (Jouncil, having its seat at New Orleans, and the
Supreme Council, then and now having its seat at Charleston, B. C.-he adhered to
the Supreme Council of Charleston, of which he was a member. At that time the
Grand Lodge of Louisiana was under the absolute control of the Supreme Council of

New Orleans, a.nd, at ita dictation, declared Bro. SNELL expelled. The act was withont jnrisdiction a.nd was a nullity, and the allege? offense was one unknown to
Masonic jurisprudence. Subsequently the Grand Lodge of Lonisia.na was re-organized and became, and has thence continued to be, an independent Grand Lodge;
a.nd when ·the unlawful act of expulsion was brought to its attention, it promptly
rescinded the act. The first act was without authority of law and was void. We
ta.ke it that Bro. SNELL, although declared expelled, never was expelled.
.
Some of the cases of hardship and injustice which have been brought to our
attention from time to time have been of like character-cases where the Master of a
Lodge has pronounced judgment of suspension against a member of his Lodge without having acquired jurisdiction ¥> pronounce any judgment. Whenever such a case
arises it is the plain duty of the Masrer to declare that the act was void. The party
declared to have been suspended was not suspended, because the Master had no
Hthority to make the dedlaration.
