Your commlttee, to whom was referred the e.ppee.l of CHA.RLEB~How.1.RD GORDON
from the action of Woodbridge Lodge, No. 131, in expelling him from e.11 the rights
and privileges of Masonry, have had the same under consideration and report as
follows:This case was before your committee at the last Annual Communication, when the
judgment of the Lodge was reversed and the case reme..nded for further. proceedings,
the ground that the accused was denie_d an opporturuty to prep~re his defense •.
00
The accused was age.in tried, and on the twenty-fifth day of Apnl, 1874, was e.ge.m
expelled from all the rights and privileges of Masonry. From this judgment and sentence he appeals, on the ground that the 1'.1e~bers of the ~dge were not legally
notified or the special meeting to elect comm1ss1oners for the trial.
.
Th transcript shows that at said special meeting there were present only mne
memb:rs, while sixty-eight were borne upon the roll. No written notices were sent
to the members, but a portion of them were verbally notified by the M3'.'ter a?d Secretary. A verbe.J notice does not constitute due notificati?n ~s proVIded m Sec. 2,
Article IV. Pe.rt VI., and in Art. II. Pe.rt VII., of the Constitution. The law defines a
notification or notice to be a "call Issued by the Secretary by ord~r of the Lodge or
Master or by other competent authority, to attend for some specific purpose at the
time a~d place indicated, or to perform some specific duty therein ~t forth." It ie
especially important that, in case a specie.I meeting of a Lodge .'s ca.lie~ for th_e
election of trial-commissioners, every member thereof whose reBidence IB known
ahould be notified, in order that jUBtice may be done to all concerned.
In this case the accused ste. tes as a further ground of appeal that two of the commissioners elected were relatives of the accuser, and the.i they, with others of the

1874:.J

Grand Lodge of California.

569

commissioners, were strongly prejudiced age.inst him. Be this as it may, the failure
to notify the members to attend the specie.I meeting for the election of the commission
renders a reverse.I of the judgment unavoidable. Your coinmittee, therefore, recommend the adoption of the following resolution:Resolved, That the action of Woodbridge Lodge, No.131, in expelling CHARLBB
How ARD GORDON from all the rights and privileges of Masonry, be reversed and set
aside, and that the case be remanded for further and more correct proceedings.

7b the M.-. W. •. Grand Lodge of Oalifornia :Yonr committee, to whom was referred the petition of lsmoR N. CHOYNBIU for
r estore.tion to the rights and privileges of Masonry, have bad the same under consideration and report as follows :The petitioner was, by order of the Grand Master, tried in .Mount .Moriah Lodge,
No. 44, in June, 1871, upon charges of nnme.sonic conduct for the reason that he,
whi]e acting as a commissioner on the trial of one Jo11N MA.GUIRB, rendered a verdict
directly at variance with the testimony adduced. Of this charge he was acquitted
and the case went np on appeal to the Grand Lodge at its Annual Communication in
October, 1871. The resnlt of this e.ppee.l was that the action of the Lodge was
reversed and set a.side, and CHOYNBKI was sUBpended from all the rights and prlvilege_s of Masonry. At the le.st Annual Communication a petition was presented to
the Grand Lodge for bis restoration, which petition was referred to a special committee who , after a careful examination of all the facts in the case, reported in Javor
of granting the prayer of the petitioner. Objections, however, having been made by
severe.I brethren of the Grand Lodge, the report of the committee was not concurred
in, and the petitioner still remains suspended.
Those obj~ctioUB having now been withdrawn by the brethren who interposed
them, he O(ICe more presents his petition to the Grand Lodge, alleging that he acted
conscientiously in the matter upon which the charges were based, and that he did
not willully violate any law of Masonry.
This may or may not be true, but your committee are of the opinion that four
yea.rs' suspension is a sufficient punishment for the offense committed; and they
therefore olfer the following resolution and recommend its adoption:Resolved, That Ismon N. CHoYNSKI, suspended by this Grand Lodge in October,
1871, be and is hereby restored to all the rights and privileges of Masonry.

C. DENSON, Grand Orator, delivered the annual address, as follows::MOST WoBSHIPFUL GRAND MASTER AND
BRETHREN OF THE GRAND LODGE : -

To us who have grown to manhood amid the resounding machinery of modem

pr~gress, it does not appear surprising that we sit to-day around the common altar

which we have established in this beautiful temple, "erected to God and dedicated
to His Holy Name;" but to onr patriot fathers who, within the p~esen~ century,
held dubious titles to their firesides and were in constant warfare with wild beasts
and savages how improbable would have st>emed a prophecy that a Grand Lodge of
Free and Ac~epted Masons would be convened, under the prese_nt circumstances, on
the verge of the western world, where the pul&ell of the Pacific ocean throb and the
setting sun takes its leave of the American continent.
.
.
· The fact that we are here to-day ib unt one more demonstration that our Order is
founded upon living principles of broad and universal application. Those vali~nt
sons of knighthood and chivalry who, in ancient times, rode forth emblazo.ned with
the crude emblems of our Order, and illuminated a dark and cruel age with deeds
of heroism and mercy, never imagined, even in their wildest dreams of roma~ce,
that the principles of justice and charity which they could ~-aintain only ~y fosten~g
the martial spirit, would survive the assaults of superstition and fiendish folly ?1
religion's guise, and finally arise triumphant and build for themselv~s temples m /
the hearts of an enlightened people to liv·e in a world to them unknown..
.
From the windows of this Grand Lodge Hall we look to-day, with pnde _and a~m1ration, upon a city grand and beautiful, teeming with life a?d rev~rberatmg w_ith a
thousand Industries-the cen\re of a large and constantly mcreasmg populationthe only eity in the world presenting the compactnesss of apparent antiqnit~ and at
the same time embellished with the symmetrical beauty of modem architec~u~e.
Upon these crowded thoroughfares the European, the Saxon, the Celt, the -~iat1c,
and the tawny sons of the isles of the ocean, meet upon a common level of
and
religions liberty, each intent upon working ont for himself the solemn problems of

m"P

life.
. .
ml
A few short years ago the site of this splendid city was a waste of shiftmg sa s.
For untold ages had the stare of heaven k ept silent watch by _the ~npeo.Ple~ portals
of the sea, while none but ships of mist rode at anchor m this beautif(il port.
It was long after the intrepid Columbus discovered and presented a n~w.J.orld to
the Queen of Castile that the first civilized man stood up on the monntams summit,
and gazed in rapturous wonder upon the placid waters of the Pacific Ocea~, and
later still when the English corsair and Spanish buccaneer dropped anchor m San
Francisc~ bay; while far up in the nineteenth century this bright land of the vine and
the fig, the shining metal and the golden haryest, was so little known that ev~n ~he
greatest of American statesmen characterized it as a land flt only for the habitation
of reptiles and beast'! of prey. The votary of an occult science looked.to t~e c~cible
of the alchemist for gold ; while, wiser and more courageous, the Cahfornia pioneer
sought and found it in the mountain's gorge in the land of the sunset. Scarcely a
quarter or a century has elapsed since this fair State was an unexplo~ed waste, aud
now no land beneath the sun is bet ter known for it'! wonderful productions or for the
enterprise and intelligence of its people.
.
.
To the accomplishment of these splendid results Masonry has contnbuted m no
small degree. Full well do we know that a firm reliance on the universall_ty and
reality of Masonic charity moved many of our bravest, wisest, and noblest pioneers

to endute the hardships and perils incident to their immigratiou and conquest of a
remote and mysterious land. Amid all the excitements and distres~P.s, all t.he moral
and political revolutions caused by the pouring in of a cosmopolitan population,
Masonry was neither forgotton nor neglected, but comtantly raised its kind and
pleading voice in solemn admonition, and undoubtedly exerted a mighty i~fluence in
moulding the destinies of and giving character to the State.
This benefl.cent work of the ).lBllt indicates that we have before us opportunities
involving high duties and presenting a field for unpreoedent.ed achievements ; while
the peat history of our society formulates this distinct proposition-The gen·i us of

Masonry is prod.ucti"llB and COflllenJatille of republican i11stitutiom.
By becoming Masons we are none the less integral parfB of the body politic, and
ea such we should carefully study our Order and ourselves in the relations that it and
we bear, collectively and individually, to the State and to our fellow-citizens. Upon
the very threshold of Masonry we are taught to "be quiet and peaceable citizens,
true to onr government and just to our country;" and "not to countenance diBloyalty or rebellion, but patiently submit to legal authority and to conform with
cheerfulness to the government of the country in which we live." Bnt this is the
bare e-qggestion of a thought to be constantly elaborated, and we, as members of an
enlightened and conservative Craft, owe it to ounelves, our Order, and the government which sanctifies our lives, protoolll our property, and approves the celebration
of our ancient rites and ceremonies., to devote untiring service to that government
and to purify, preserve, and protect it from political ga•grene and decay.
And here, lest my position be misunderstood, I take occasion to declare that I
would not have our excellent Order become a political body or interfere in partizan
issues. I am proud to say that from time immemorial the Masonic lodge-room has
been a sanctuary where.the disturbing elements of partizan politics could not enter
to mar its fraternal harmony; but ea men and citizens we have ever enjoyed the
broadest discretion in the exercise of individual duty to the State. I am not of those
who believe that the world is growing worse, nor do I believe that wickedness is
the hand-maid of enligMenment; but with the present ?acilities for the transmission of
news we hear more of current gossip. The unusual and remarkable incident attracts
attention, so that more is said, thought, and written of one vile act than of ten
thousand noble and virtuous deeds which should invoke the. applanding smiles of
angelic hosts.
We have no right to justify ourselves by the standard of the past. We claim to be
wiser than our predecessors, and onght to be better and purer than they. In the
midst of all our intelligence, crime, like a grim demon, stalks through the land; error
goes capering through the highways and by-ways; and corruption, like the obscene
vulture, sits unbidden at the public feast and threatens to taint and pollute what it
does not destroy. So long as these thing3 exist our field of labor is extensive, and we
mnst not sit idly by the wayside and see the clouds of error obscure the warming rays
of freedom's light. A vigorons and concerted eft'ort should be made by our benevoleut Fraternity to foet.er, mould, and create In the public mind sentiments of honor,
patriotism, and self-sacrificing devotion to the aft'airs of State.
Governments are merely tl1e compacts of the people for mutual benefit-an
extended family-a cooperation of the multitude for the benefit and protection of the
individuals; and to say that a government is corrupt , as Hach, is tantamount to an
assertion that the maBB of the people composing tile same is corrupt, or so neglectful
of vital interests as to permit a vicious and polluted minority to hold the reins of
power. The character and nature of a government will depend upon the virtue,
intelligence, bravery, and patriotic zeal of itll subjects. No good government can
exist among a debauched and wicked people, and no bad one can long hold sway
over a virtuous and intelligent people. Then the most direct means of securing a
good government is by an infusion of the proper spirit into the minds of the m&BBes;

1.b the M.·. w.·. Grand Lodge of Oali/brnia:Bro. ARraUR E. HILL aska if, "when the Grand Lodge sends a case back to a
Lodge for a new trial, the persons who served as commissioners on the first trial may
be elected and serve as commissioners for the new trial." Your committee have considered the question and are of the opinion that no person who acted as commissioner
on the first is competent to sit as a commissioner on the second trial. He has heard
the evidence and has made up his mind deliberately as to the guilt er ilmocence of
the acclll!ed, and it would be idle to say that he is a properpenion to serve as a commissioner on the second trial, against the objection or either party. The first qoaliflcatlon
of a commissioner should be that he can and will determine the case according to the
~vidence that shall be produced on the trial and to the law applicable thereto, as
declared by the Master. That he could not do if he had prejudged the case.

further provided, as e.n equitable adjustment, that, !J'om the date when the money
was originally paid in, the parties should be credited with interest upon the surplus in

.A.t the stated meeting in July, 1873, certain members of the Lodge moved to correct

The memorie.lists pray the Grand Lodge to give the matter such attention e.s It

the Lodge e.od its members.
It is evident to your committee that' this Lodge has embarrassed itself by the careless me.oner in which it has transacted its business. The -memorialis'i.. are mistaken
10 their representation that the Lodge adopted e. by-law amending Sec 1, Art. IX, of
the uniform code. It was only the adoption of a proposition to amend. There is
nothing in the records of the ollice or the Gre.ud Secretary which shows that the
Lodge perfected what it proposed in 1867. On the contrary, the lett.er of the Grand
Master at that time records the fact that a proposed amendment was submitted to
him, embodying ·life-membership, from which he withheld his approval, and it was
returned to the Lodge. We have no evidence of any further action in the matter
beyond what appears in the memorial. It is due to the Lc;dge to say that the Grand
Master, in returning the proposed amendment, gave e.o intimation (because the precedent had been established), that a well digested and carefully considered plan of
life-membership might be accomplished by the adoption of resolutions to that effect,
doly recorded ; but, there is no evidence that the Lodge a tlached special imp.:irtance
to the suggestion, or that it took any further action upon the return of the proposed
amendment. and we necessarily conclude that none was had.
The opinion of the committee is that the system of life-membership and the issue
of certificates practiced by Colusa Lodge, No. l!l2, is iorormal and imperfect ;. and
that the by-law referred to remains as It .was in 1867, unaltered and unamended.
The committee consider it their duty to go further into the case in order to reach
the prayer of the memorialists. It is apparent that the belief pervaded t he Lodge
tluit the system of life-membership was legally established, and noder tuis impression
the Lodge and its members acted in good faith, e.od contracts were entered into
between them. The existence of this opinion and its strength is indicated by the
resolution adopted at the stated meeting iu Mdy, 1873, although we do not think
much of the legal force of that resolution, and it now becomes e. quest ion with us as
Me.sons, whether rights accrued under a contract entered Into between a Lodge and its
members in good faith, in violation of no principle and unimpeached by any allegation which can .mar the integrity of the act. ought to be annulled or disturbed by the
supreme authority without the mutual consent of the contracting parties, even if
legal technicalities have not been literally complied with. Although there may be a
ditterent principle governing in politica.l law, ~e do not believe that It should apply
to us; and especially where a Lodge has bound itself by its high act, in a contract
with its members, it should be held to it until fulfilled or released from it.
The opinion of the committee is 'that C'olusa Lodge, No. U2, is honorably bonod
by its contract with those members to whom it has issued its certificates of life-membership, discharging them from further payment of monthly dues so long as they
remain members of that Lodge, or choose to hold the Lodge tiound.

This proposed regulation was intended to meet a difficulty which has constantly

hearing verbal evidence, statements, and arguments in cases before. them on ap~.
The Gra.nd Lodge must render final judgment in all those cases, and it has determmed
that additional evidence may be given whenever the partiee deeire to introduce more
than was heard at the trial before the commisaiooers. The resolution proposes that
this evidence shall be reduced to writing, and shell be put in at least sixty days before
the ineetiog of the Gra.nd Lodge. This is right. If such testimony is deemed neces811ry, it is proper that it should be presented in time to give the commi~ an oppor.
tunity to examine it, and it is very reasonable that none should be put m later than
sixty days before the meeting of the Grand Lodge.
·

ought to have its reports prepared before the commencement or the Communication\
--certainly ought not to be interrupted during the session by being compelled to hear
t.estimouy or argument. Your committee, therefore, recommend that the proposed
resolution be adopted.

their judgment, he h118 such right and that the constitution ought to provide the

way in which be may exercise it. It is plain that any one who has prejudged the
oase, or w~o has any personal ill will or enmity towe.rds the accused, or who is
strongly b1118ed or prejudiced either for or against him, oaght not to be allowed to
serve as & commissioner to try him. He could not give the pa.rty a. fa.ir trial, and
true verdict render a.ccording to the law and.the evidence.
There are certain fundamental principles of justice and right that underlie and
control 11ll legiel11tive enactments. Of these we may mention tha.t no man can sit as
judge in his own case; that the accuser can never be allowed to try the acco.aed; that
one who has prejudged 11 case oannot sit in judgment in that case. Onr common
sense of justice would revolt at any one of these things; and ~o one would hesitate
to pronounce any law, which should provide for any one of them, to be in derogation
of the inherent and insliena.ble right. of man, and therefore void.
The commission before which 11 Mll800 is to be tried, as the court before which
any man is to be tried, or by which his rights are to be detAlrmintd, should be compos~ of ~hose who can and will do even justice; and it would be 11 mockery to say
that it might be composed of those who were personally hostile to the party io be
tried, or who had prejudged his case. If any person should be elected ag a commissioner, whose mind W118 so bi1111ed or prejudiced by reason of unfriendly.personal
relations, or a.ny other cause, that he ought not, 118 an honorable man, to serve on
the trial, it is the a.beolute right of the accneed to object and to show cause for bia
objection at any time before the trial commences, unless the time for making objeotion is limited by positive enactment; and It would be the duty of the Vaster to heat"
and determine the objection, and, if he found it well taken, io exclude the party
against whom it waa made from participation in the trial: and furlher, if such
objection were found to be well taken against a majority of the commissioners their
election should be vacated·a.nd & new one for the rejected oommissioners be ordered.
If the trial commi•sioners were appointed·by the Mast.er, instead of' being elected
by the Lodge, it would be a comparatively simple matter for objections to be made
and dispolled of. But our law provides for their election by the Lodge; and, 1111 we
think, neceese.rily implies that the qualifications of each one nominated for election
may be canvassed and inquirecl'int.o at the time, and t.b&t it would be entil'ely proper
for th~ Master to require the attendance of the accused at such meeting, to inierpoee
objeet10ns to any one proposed· for elootion, if he desired io do so; and that the
Master might very properly determine the suflioienoy of the objections. and the
qualiftoatione of the party n~ed for election before the election proceeds..
If the case be one in which t!.te Master is personally intemited io such extent
that be would be disqwilifted as a. commissioner, he is disqualified to preside ai the

To the M. ·• W. •• Grand Lodge of California:your committee have carefully considered the matter submitted to them in the
Address of the Grand Master, upon the petition t'<\r a dlspeneation to form a Lodge

Your committee, to whom was yesterday recommitted their report upon the
a~peal of JOHN F. HARRIS from the action of Orocket.t Lodge, No. 139, in suspending
him from all the rights and privileges of Masonry, after further con•ideration, now
present the following:-

•
'

•

This is a case o~ ~lander alleged to have been circulated by Bro. JOHN F. HARRIS,
~ member of Benicia Lodge, No. 5, but resident of San Francisco, againsp Bro.
UHARLES McCoRincx, Madter of OrockeU Lodge, No. 139. The proceedings in the
case seem to be. regul~r, all the requirements of the Constitution in regard io trials
ID such cases ha v~g been observed; and, after a full hearing, the commission adjudged
the defendant guilty as charged in several of the specifications and sentenced him
to suspension from all the rights and privileges of Masopry.
Without expressing any opinion as to the merits of the case, or the evidence elicited to sustain the charges upon the investigation held, your committee believe that
there is a. principle involved in the subject under consideration which directly
affe~ts, and• might serionsly prejudice, the rights of any Mason in the jurisdiction
aga1Dst whom charges may be preferred for copdnct olfensive to the Master of a
Lodge.
After a careful examination of the transcript, and a fair construction of the alleged
offense :.nd of the defen~e contained therein, your committee conclude that Bro.
CHABL~S ~cCORHICx, Master of Orocket{ Lodge, is a party directly interested in the
~et~rnunatio~ of. the charges against Bro. JOHN F. HARRIS; and that, being a party
ID 1Dterest, It was not proper for OrockeU Lodge to determine a matter at isene ·
between its Master a.nd a member of another Lodge.
;nie constitution will not permit a Lodge to try its Master; and, as a Lodge should
b~ ID natural sympathy wi~ its Master and directly interested in the preservation of
his good name and fame, 1t should not be permttted to decide a matter at issue
between him a~d a Mason not a member, as a· verdict of acquittal would justify the
defendant and imply the truth of the alleged slander. Believing, therefore, that, in
justice to both parties, this issue shonld be removed to a .tribunal not only disinterested, but not to be iu the least affected by the verdict, yonr committee submit the
following resolution and recommend its adoption:~
Resolved, That the action of Orockett Lodge, No. 139, in suspending Bro. JOHN F.
HARRIS from all the rights and privileges of Masonry, be and the same is hereby

To the M. ·• W. •• Grand Lodge of California :Your committ.ee, to whom was referred the appeal of Bro. FRANCIS FOSTER from
the action of Union Lodge, No. 58, in acquitting Bro. W1LLLU1 S. HUNT of certain
charges preferred against him, have had the same under consideration and report as
follows:In this case it has tome to the knowledge of your committ.ee that the testimony
of the witnesses at the trial was not written out by the brother acting as Secretary,
(Bro. HUNT, the accused, being Secretary of the Lodge,) but that, by direction of the
commissioners, only brief notes thereof were taken, which notes were afterwards
destroyed and the rocord was made up by the acting Secretary from memory. This,
of itself, would afford aiy.ple ~ound to justify a reversal of the action of the Lodge;
but there is a much more serious feature of this case which, in the opmion of your
committee, calls for prompt and decisive action on the part of this Grand Body.
It appears that, after the record was made up by the acting Secretary, was certified
by him under the seal of the Lodge, and was by him placed in the post.cflice at Sacramento, directed to the Grand Secreta~ the defendant, Bro. HUNT, learning that
the transcript had been placed in the post office, went to the postmaster and, by
falsely representing that a letter written b"JI himself was dropped in the post-office on
that d&y, obtained the transcript; and then, by and with the consent and assistance
of the Master, altered said transcript by eliminating a portion thereof and eublftituting four pages which were not in the original as certified to by.the actinl{ Becretarythe Master then certifying that such altered record wa9 correct. Your committ.ee are
of the opinion that by this act Bro. WILLIAM S. HmiT h8.'I not only committed a
Masonic offense, but one :which, under the laws of the land, would be construed as a
felony; and they cannot too strongly condemn the action of the Master who, by
aiding and abetting such a transaction, has laid himself liable to charges of unmasonic conduct, which cllJIJ"ges will, at the proper time, be preferred by your committ.ee. They now only reco~mend the adoption of the following resolution :-

From the foregoing statement it will be seen that at the present Communication
one hundred and seventy-five chartered Lodges were represented, being all 'save
sixteen, together with six of the seven Lodges acting under dispensation. It will also be
seen that to forty-one Lodges no allowance has been made. Of these, eighteen-being
Nos. ".I., 17, 22, 30, «, 61, US, 120, 127, 136, 1S9, 166, 169, 188, 212, 215, 216, and 219though they were represented and their dues were paid, are located in this city or its
immediate vicinity; sixteen-being Nos.14,.S2, 34, 100, 105, 129, 1S3, 135, 141, 1«,
198, 200, 213, 214, 225, and Surprise Valllly, U. D., have paid their dues bot have not
been represented at all; four-being Nos.115, 175, i94, and 221-have paid their dues
but were not represented on the first day, as our law requires, and were not excused ;
and three-being Nos. 21, 177, and 22S, are located with.out the State and are not
chargeable with dues to this fund or entitled to, receive anything therefrom. It will
be observed, also, that allowances have been made to several Lodges which were
not represented on the first day of the Communication, viz.: Nos. 18, 41, 55, 106, 117,
208, and 211, the representatives thereof having been excused by the Grand Lodge
for the lateness of their attendance.

showed that a ml\iority of the votes for Master had been cast for the then Master, who
was not present. A Past Master of the Lodge, presiding at the ttme, suggested that
the brother w·ho had thus received a majority of the votes, and was re-elected Master,
was absent and would not probably return in time for the installation, and that he
would entertain a motion to reconsider the ballot. A motion to that effect was tnereupon made and.declared carried, and another ballot was had which showed a majority
ofvotee for an<>ther brother for the office of Master. The Grand Master held that the
brother who had received a majority of the votes cast at the 1lret ballot was duly
eleeted, and that it was not competent for the Lodge to re-consider each a ballot.
If for any reason the Master elect should fail to appear for installation within a
reBBenable period, the L<>dge will find a remedy in Sec. 1, Art. I, Part II, and Sec.
2, Art. I, Part IV, of the Constitution.

'To which Past Grand Master PRATT responded as follows : MosT WORSHll'FUL Sm AND BRETHREN OF THE GB.A.ND LODGE:
All a.long the journey of life, however unfortunate may be ita general course,
there come some pleasant passages, the memories of which will ~er to light up
after years with divine and hallowed radiance; and I am to-day in the midst of one
of those experiences.
Men a.re born for. thought and e.ction, and toil in a noble cause is sweet, be.it of
the head, the heart, or the hand. It is sweet, too, to receive the substa.ntia.l rewe.rds
of labor-sweeter still to be assured that our efforts have been crowned witb some
measure of success-but dearer than all is the approbation, the gratitude, and the
love of those in whose behalf our energies have been expended.
The intrinsic value of this magnificent testimonial bespeaks the kindness a.nd
generosity of those who he.ve been charged with its selection and preps.ration, and I
am too practical to ignore its uses and its value. , But while I would accept it grate-

ARTICLE I.
OF ITS TITLB ..UID BEAL.

SBOTION 1. Tbl~ Grand Lodge shall be entitled "The Most Worsbipfal Grand

AltTICL'E II.
OF ITS MEMBERS AND THEIR QUALJFIOATIONB.

SECTION 1. The Grand Lodge shall be composed of a Grand Master, (whose

ARTICLE V.
OF !TB ELECTIONS A.ND APPOINTMENTS,

.ARTICLE ill.

SECTION 1. The Grand Master, Deputy Grand Master, Grand Wardens, Grand
Treasurer, and Grand Secretary shall bo el11cted by ballot, at each Annual Communication, upon the fourth day thereof; shall be installed before its close; and aha.II ho41
their respective offices until their successors shall have been elected and installed. A majority of all the votes cast shall be necessary for an election.
SEO. 2. All other Grand Officers shall be appointed by the Grand Master, immediately after his installation, at each Annual Communication ; shall be properly
invested before the close thereof; and shall hold their respective offices during his
will and pleasure.
SEo. 3. Whenever a vacancy shall occur in any elective office of the Grand
Lodge, the Grand Master shall have power to fill the same by appointment, which
appointment shall be valid until the succeeding annual election and installation ; and
the officer so appointed shall be charged with all the duties and responsibilities of
one regularly elected.

OF ITS POWERS A.ND AUTHORITY.

SEOTIOI' I. The Grand Lodge is the Supreme Masonic Power and Authority in
·this State, possessing all the attributes of sovereignty and government-legislative,
executive, and judicial-limited only by a strict adherence to the Ancient Landmarks
of the brder, and by the provisions of its own Constitution and Regulations.
SEC. 2. Its legislative powers extend to every case of legislation not expressly
delegated by itself to the Lodges; and the Constitutions and Regulations, which it
has an inalienable right to adopt and promulgate at its own convenience, and to alter,
amend or repeal at its own pleasure, under the limitations therein imposed, are final
and blnding upon all Lodges and ~ wilJWL i'8 ior.iadicW>n. until so altered,
amended, or repeal&
Ssc. 3. Its executive powers inclu(ie the granting of dispensationli and charters
to establish and perpetuate Lodges within this State, and in other territory where
no Grand Lodge exists; the revocation or suspension thereof; the issuiug of special
dispensations for all purposes permitted by any of the provisions of this Constitution;
and the exercise, generally, of all such authority as may be necessary to carry its
own legislation into complete eflect.
SEO. 4. Its judicial powers are o~ two kinds:let. Original-Including the decision of all controversies between any of the
Lodges, or between one of them and a member or members of another; and the
enforcement ol' discipline upon its own members and upon the Lodges under its
jurisdiction: and
.
2d. Appellate-Embracing the revision of all matters of controversy or discipline,
proper for Masonic investigation, which may have arisen in any of the Lodges, and
over which it has not retained original jurisdiction.
ARTICLE IV.
OF ITS CO:.WUNICA.TJONS.

SEoTION 1. · The Grand Lodge shall hold its Annual Communications, for the
tranSllction of its regular business, at the Vity of San ~'rancisco, commencing on the
second Tuesday of October, at 10 o'clock, A. M.
SEO. 2. Special Communications may be ordered by the Grand Master whenever,
in his opinion, the welfare of the Fraternity shall require it.
::!EC. 3. ::lpecial IJommuuications shlLil be ordered by the Grand Master upon an
application therefor in writing, setting forth the causes which demand it, and signed
by the Masters of at least tilteen chartered Lodges.
S11:c. 4. Every order- for a Speoial Communication shall designate the object
thereof, so far as is proper to be written, and, unless such Communication be called
merely for the performance of some Masonic ceremony, shall be issued to each Lodge
and Grand Officer at lea.st thirty days before the day named for meeting; and no
business ·shall be transacted thereat other than that tor which the Grand Lodge was
especially convened.
SEO. 6. The officers or representatives of at least seventy-five chartered Lodges
shall be present in order to transact any business in the Grand Lodge, either at an
Annual or Special Communication; but, upon occasions of ceremony only, the Grand
Alaster, or his duly authorized repre_sentative, with a sufficient number of brethren to
fill the stations and places, may at any time open the Grand Lodge and _perform the
ceremonies for which it was convened.
•
BEd. 6. None but members of the Grand Lodge (the Grand Officers, Past Grand
Officers, or Representatives of other Grand Lodges, and th~ members of the .Grand
Organist's choir, excepted) shall be present at the operung thereof or durmg an
election the1'8in.

ARTlCLE VI.
OF ITS VOTING AND REI'BESENTA.TION,

~

r

SECTION 1. All questions in the Grand Lodge, except elections of officers, shall
be decided either viva voce or by a show of hands ; unless, before the announcement
of the result thereof, three members ~hall demand that the vote be taken by yeBs and
nays, in which case it shall thus be taken.
SEo. 2. Each Grand Officer present, whether elected or appointed, (except the
Graiid Tyler,) and each Past Grand Officer present, shall be entitled to one vote.
SEC. 3. Each Lodge represented shall be entitled to three votes; and the Past
Masters of each Lodge shall, collectively, be entitled to one vote.
SEC. 4. No Grand Officer, Past Grand Officer, or Past Master, voting, or participating in a vote, in either of those capacities, shall vote, or participate in a vote, in
any other of them; but either of such members may, as Master, Warden, or representative of a Lodge, cast also the vote or votes to which such position shall entitle
him.
SEO. 5. When a Lodge shall be represented by only two of its proper officers,
the officer highest in rank may cast two of its three votes.
BEc. 6. When a Lodge shall be represented by ouly one of Its proper officers,
or by a representative, such officer or representative may cast all the votes to which
it is entitled.
SEO. 7. In all cases of a tie vote, except votes by ballot, the Grand Master, in
addition to his proper vote, may have the casting vote.
ARTICLE VII.
OF ITS COMMITTEES A.ND TREIB DUTIES,

BEcrION 1. The following regular committees, to consist of five members each
shall be appointed by the Grand Master at each Annual Comm~ication, as soon W:
practicable alter its commencement, viz.: On Credentials, on Finances, on Chartel'll,
and on By-Laws of Lodges, the duties of which committees shall cease at the close of
such Communication.
SJW. 2. The following standing committe~s, to consist of five members each
shall also be appointed by the Grand Master at each Annual Communication, jus~
before Its close, viz.: On Jurisprudence, on Grievances, on Correspondence, and on
Returns, the duties of which committees shall continue during the year thereafter,
and shall cease at the close of tJ,ie next succeeding .A.nnual Communication.

Grand Wardens shall, in the order of their rank, succeed to and be charged with all
the powers and duties of the Grand Master.

SECTION I. The powers and duties or a Lodge are such as are prescribed in its
dispensation or charter, by the Constitution and Regufa:tioos of the Grand Lodge, and
by the general regulations of Masonry; and they are defined as follows :1st. E.recuti·v e-In the direction and performance of its work, as prescribed by
· the Grand Lodge, under the contml of the Master; and in all other matters, in aid of
the Master, who is the primary executive authority of the Lodge:
2d. Legislative-Including all matters of legislation relative to i~ internal concerns, which shall not be in violation of the general regulations of Masonry, the Constitution or Regulations of the Grand Lodge, or its own particular by-laws: and
3d. JudiciaZ- Embraqing the exercise of discipline over its own members (except
the Master) and all other Masons within its jurisdiction, and the settlement of controversies between them; subject always to a revision by the Grand Lodge upon
appeal.
SEo. 2. E ach Lodge shall have not more than one stated meeting in each lunar

of Masier Masons.

GENERAL REGULATIONS,
AS REMAINING AFTER THE REVISION OF THE CONSTITUTION
In October, 1874.

1. This Grand Lodge recognizes no degree of Past Master conferred by any
authority not holden under a legitimate Gran(! Lodge-acknowledging only the Order
of that name as it exists in the ceremonies attenditlg the installation of the Master
elect of a chartered Lodge; which Order shall be conferred only by a convocation
of Present° or Past Masters, not less than three In number, who have tbns regularly
-received it.
2. All Masonic communication between the Lodges and Masons of this jnris·
diction and those acknowledging allegiance to the Grand Lodge of Hamburg, is
l;tereby forbidden, while that body shall continne Its nnlawfnl and reprehensible
Invasion of the jurisdictional rights of the Grand Lodge of New J'ork.
S. Such standard of revenne shall be continued hereafter as will alford an annual
excess over the current expenditures of at least one thousand dollars; which exceBB
shall each year be set aside, as an accnmnlating fond, to be known as the Reserve
Fund, which shall be kept and increased for purposes of emergency, and shall only
be drawn upon therefor. At each Annual Communication, a Board of Trustees, three
in number, shall be elected, whose duty it shall be judicionsly to invest all moneys
set aside for such fund, and all moneys accruing from the interest on such investmen\s;
and each member of said Board shall execute and file in the office of the Grand Secretary, a bond in the penal snm of $5000, to be appr~ved by the Grand Master, Grand
Treasurer, a.od Grand Secretary, conditioned that he will faithfnlly perform the duties
of his tni$\.
4.. No Lodge under this jurisdiction shall be allowed to transact bosioe11s, other
than the conferring of degrees, with a less ·number than seven members present.
5. The Grand Secretary is authorized to charge ibe sum of one dollar, for the nse
of the Grand Lodge, for each copy of its printed proceedings for the current year,
other than the four copies to be sent to each subordinate Lodge, and those required
for transmission abroad, for fntnre binding, and for the nae of the Grand Lodge at its
next sncoeeding Annual Oommnnication.
.
6. All Masons, heretofore stricken from the rolls of Lodges within this jurisdiction
for non-payment of dues, who have not been reinstated, are hereby deolared to be
suspended, as provided in Sec. 11, Art. Ill, Part Ill, of the Constitution.
7. Io addition to the dues prescribed in the Constitution, there shall be levied
hereafter npon the subordinate Lodges, for each Master Mason whose name is borne
npon their rolls at the date of the annual returns, snc.h sum as the Grand Loc'ge shall
prescribe at each Anonal Commnnicatiou, ll:hich shall constitute a special fund to be
denominated "The Representative Fund;" and It shall be the duty of the several
Lodges to pay the said sum at the time and in the manner directed in the Constitution
for the payment of their annual dnee,

646

General RegulatiOrllJ of tlie

1874.]

[Oct.,

8. At the cloRe of each Annual Communication, a committee, to be known as the
"Committee on Pay of Members" and to consist ot five, shall be appointed by the
Grand Master, whose dnty It shall be to ascertain, during the year succeeding, the
exact cost of transportation for one person from the location of each Lodge in the
State to the place of meeting of the Grand Lcidge and back again ; and, at the fol·
lowing Annual Communication, to report snch cost of transportation a• the sum due
to the officers or representative in attendance from each chartered Lodge, which sum ·
shall be paid by the Grand Treasurer, •nch report being his voucher therefor. But
no pllyment shall be allowed for the ofttcers or representative of any Lodge, the dues
of which shall not have been paid In foll.
•
9. The appointed Grand Officers and the chairmen of standing committees shall
receive payment for their necessary expenditures for transportation to a:id from
each Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge, In the same manner as ordered for
the oflicers or representatives of Lodites; bot no Grand Officer, chairman, or officer
or representative of a Lodge, shall receive such payment i11 more than one or those
capacities, nor shall he receive it unless be shall have been In attendance at such
Communication from the first to the last day thereof, inclnsive, unless excused by the
Grand Lodge.
10. The work and lectures presented by the committee appointed for their exam·
ination and revision, are approved, adopted, and made obligatory upon 'an Lodges
within this jnrisdictiou; and any Lodge which shall have had Qpportunity to obtain
instruction therein, and shall neglect or refuse to learn and use the same, shall, npon
representation of that fact to the Grand Master, be liable to the arrest of its cltarter,
If, in his discretion, he shall think It proper.
11. The person who desires to be made a Mason must be a man; no woman nor
ennucb; freeborn, being neither a slave nor the eon of a bond woman ; a believer in
God and a fnture existence; of moral conduct; capable of reading and writing ; not
deformed or dismembered, but hale and sound in his physical conformation, having
his right limbs as a man ought to have; and able to conform lueraUy to what the
several degrees respectively require of him.
12. All Ma•onic intercourse between this Grand Lodge and the Grand Orient of
France Is here by suspended, and the Lodges and Masons of this jurisdiction are for·
bidden to recognize or hold communication with any brother who bails from or
acknowledges allegiance to the Grand Orient of France, so long as that body con·
tinues its unlawful and reprehensible invasion of the jurisdictional rights of the
Grand Lodge of Louisiana.
13. No Master of a Lodge shall be installed until be shall have produced to the
lnstalllng officer the certificate of the Grand Lecturer, or of the Inspector of the
District In which such Lodge Is situated, that he ls qualified to give the work and
lectures entire in the three degrees; and such certificate, lndorsed by the installing
oftlcer, shall be forwarded by him to the Grand Lecturer, to be kept on file 'in Jlis
